title: Buffalo Bills trending up, trending down: The players who will decide game at Jets
summary: The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (32.0) and total yards per game (386.4), and they head to MetLife at 7-1 on a four-game winning streak. The Jets are 2-7 and have lost four in a row, which makes this look like a game that plays itself. Joe Brady spent the week telling […]
full_text: The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (32.0) and total yards per game (386.4), and they head to MetLife at 7-1 on a four-game winning streak. The Jets are 2-7 and have lost four in a row, which makes this look like a game that plays itself. Joe Brady spent the week telling reporters that records can mislead in this league, and New York gives him some material: the NFL’s fifth-highest pressure rate (39.2 percent), 22 sacks, and a rookie in David Bailey, the second overall pick, who is tied for fourth in sacks (7.5) and tied for the league lead in forced fumbles (five). (Spencer Brown, Buffalo’s starting right tackle, is doubtful with an ankle injury.) Buffalo’s last two wins, 36-10 over the Ravens and 23-6 in Minnesota, were its two biggest of the season, and the defense gave up 16 points across both. That unit had allowed 29 or more points in five of its first six games, so the last two weeks matter. The question mark is the quarterback list: Carson Wentz, and a Ravens group that got one pass from Lamar Jackson. Geno Smith isn’t a world beater by any means, but he is an experienced starting QB in this league, with some real young talent around him. If they’re allowed to get hot and enjoy the game, it can turn into a tough afternoon for Buffalo very quickly. Without further ado, here are the players I believe will need to be at their best so the Bills can earn their eighth win of the season: KEEP ROLLING James Cook, RB: If you feed him, he’ll come James Cook carried 31 times for 107 yards and a touchdown in Minneapolis, 10 more carries than any other running back in Week 9. He averaged 2.7 yards per carry through three quarters behind Tylan Grable and Austin Corbett on the left side, then the Vikings’ front wore down: 47 yards on one fourth-quarter possession that ended with his five-yard touchdown, and Buffalo held the ball for 42:32 to Minnesota’s 17:28. PFF still graded him 52.9, a reminder that the yardage came on volume more than clean running. The Jets are the kind of defense volume works against. They rank 26th against the run at 128.0 yards per game, and it is getting worse: about 118 per game through five weeks, just over 140 over the last four. Kansas City ran for 163 yards at 5.1 yards per carry last Sunday. The advanced numbers disagree on the details, so I’ll flag it: the Jets are ninth in EPA per rush allowed (-0.142), which strips out garbage time, yet 30th in rush success rate allowed (51.5 percent). That reads to me like a defense that gives up steady, unspectacular gains, and those add up late. On the other hand, Cook is fifth in the NFL with 814 rushing yards, tied for eighth at 4.8 per carry, and he has scored in seven straight games. Since 2021, the Jets have allowed the Bills 145 rushing yards per game, 4.6 per carry, and 15 touchdowns across ten meetings, per the Jets’ own site. The one thing that can interrupt this is the football itself. That same site notes Cook has fumbled ten times since the start of last season (I flagged it in Week 6), and Bailey’s five forced fumbles lead the league. If Cook holds on to it, I expect a 25-carry day that gets better as it goes. Ed Oliver, DT: Win the one-on-ones Deone Walker gives you Ed Oliver has played five games this season, and the defense looks different with him in them. Through the first stretch, Buffalo allowed 25.3 points per game with him on the field and 31.7 without; in the two games since his return, it allowed 10 and 6. In Minneapolis, he played 28 snaps (58 percent), had three quarterback hits and graded 79.1 at PFF, the fifth-best mark on the defense. A PFF-based breakdown from The IDP Show has him at 11 pressures over those two games with no sacks and a 72.1 pass-rush grade for the season. Oliver has been around for a while now, but something has changed — Deone Walker, the nose tackle, was double-teamed on 71 percent of defensive snaps while Oliver was out, and he has earned the attention with an 86.1 PFF pass-rush grade (second among 126 qualifying interior linemen), 25 pressures and a spot on PFF’s midseason All-Pro second team. His run-defense grade is 61.9, 41st at the position, but the eye test certainly gives me some “he’s been better than this” vibes. With Breece Hall back from his quadriceps injury (15 carries for 61 yards last week) and Braelon Allen fourth in the league in rushing yards over expected (+124) and sixth at 5.0 per carry, I expect the Walker-Oliver combo to be at their best on Sunday. STEP UP Tylan Grable, OT: Back on the right side, with Bailey ahead Spencer Brown did not practice Thursday or Friday and is doubtful. I expect Grable at right tackle, with Dawkins back at left tackle and Anderson at left guard; Dawkins (ribs) and Anderson (ankle) both practiced fully on Friday and carry no designation. Right has been his best side. Before Minneapolis, most of his work had come there, including 82 snaps against Baltimore in his first real start, where charting-based metrics hit him with two pressures on 42 pass-blocking snaps, both in true pass sets. Against the Vikings, he moved to left tackle for all 80 snaps, and PFF graded him 51.0 overall with a 40.2 pass-blocking grade and four pressures allowed. PFF had him at 55.8 for the season over 133 snaps before that game. Bailey is the problem, though. He has 40 pressures on 194 rushes (20.6 percent, second-highest among players with at least 100), plus the sacks and the forced fumbles. PFF is less impressed by how he wins: a 10.3 percent pass-rush win rate (56th of 91 edge rushers) and a 66.0 pass-rush grade (38th). That gap suggests a rusher who finishes plays and benefits from the pressure around him more than one who beats tackles clean every snap, which is a matchup a swing tackle can survive. Brady said the Jets move Bailey around the formation, so it could be more about quickly recognizing stunt games and where the pressure is coming from, than simply neutralizing the man lining up in front of you. Allen was sacked four times in Minneapolis, and the bar for Grable is keeping Bailey from ending drives: no sacks, and no strips that reach the ball. Amani Hooker, S: The best moment for a new safety to arrive The Bills sent a 2027 second-round pick to Tennessee on Tuesday for Amani Hooker and a fifth, after releasing C.J. Gardner-Johnson, and Hooker said Wednesday he would play Sunday. He arrives with five interceptions, tied for the NFL lead and the most of any safety, three of them against Joe Burrow in Week 8. PFF has him at 81.0 overall, 75.2 in coverage (10th among 100 safeties) and 83.9 against the run (10th), and he played 99 percent of the Titans’ snaps across seven games. Buffalo’s defense had six interceptions through eight games and allowed 238.8 passing yards per game, the fourth-most in the league, with 28 completions of 20-plus yards. He doesn’t need to be the savior, though. The timing helps. The defense has allowed 10 and 6 points in its last two games, with six sacks over two weeks, and a new safety fits more easily on a unit that is already playing fast. Cole Bishop played all 48 snaps in Minneapolis, Damar Hamlin played 44, and Geno Stone 25, so the first thing to watch is who gives up snaps to Hooker. The test is Garrett Wilson, who leads the Jets with 527 yards and three touchdowns and practiced fully on Friday after a concussion, plus rookie Omar Cooper Jr. (306 yards and two touchdowns in five games, with an 83.3 percent catch rate. Jim Leonhard said the Jets create clean pictures for Smith and get the ball out. A safety with Hooker’s range and run-defense grade is supposed to muddy those pictures and shrink the explosive plays, and if he does it in his first game, the case for the trade makes itself. HONORABLE MENTIONS Also Rolling Connor McGovern, C: PFF graded him 75.5 in Minneapolis, fourth-best on the offense, with Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson both out against the league’s heaviest-blitzing defense. The Jets rank fifth in pressure rate, and McGovern was limited…

full_text: The Buffalo Bills have made a few internal transactions ahead of their Week 10 game against the Jets inside MetLife Stadium. And each of these moves come with some intrigue: Roster moves: – Activated DB Jordan Hancock from Injured Reserve – Released DB Te’Cory Couch – Elevated QB Shane Buechele from the practice squad — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 14, 2026 Hancock had a tremendous summer at training camp and the preseason but has been out since Week 2 with what clearly was a pretty serious hamstring injury. Suddenly, the Bills have plenty of safety depth in their secondary. As for Couch, this was somewhat of a surprising release given how well he played against the Ravens in Week 8. Because he’s still within his first four years in the NFL, he’s subject to waivers. If Couch clears waivers, the Bills will have the opportunity to place him back on their practice squad. As for the Buechele elevation — there’s no indication Josh Allen nor Kyle Allen are dealing with injuries. But now Buechele can be designated the emergency third quarterback, even if he’s inactive. Are the Bills attempting to get him a game check? I really don’t know. Your guess is as good as mine there.

full_text: The Buffalo Bills traded for safety Amani Hooker earlier this week and were apparently in on two other big names who were eventually moved before the NFL trade deadline. In Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport’s trade deadline notebook, they wrote on Buffalo’s interest in Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates, both of whom were dealt to the Jaguars: “The Jaguars and Bills will be in competition to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, but both were in competition for some of the same players ahead of Tuesday’s trade deadline. The two teams that were most aggressive in trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis were the Bills and Jaguars, who wound up trading a first- and second-round pick to the Eagles. The two teams most aggressive for former Falcons safety Jessie Bates also were the Bills and Jaguars, who traded second- and fifth-round picks to Atlanta.” They later went on to write that after the Jaguars trades, the Bills pivoted to Cardinals safety Budda Baker and Hooker. Time will tell if Jacksonville or Buffalo made the right decisions at this year’s deadline. How do you feel about this report from the league’s two biggest insiders? Do you wish the Bills swung a deal for Davis and/or Bates or are you glad Brandon Beane and Co. landed on Hooker?

title: 5 Buffalo Bills to watch at the New York Jets
summary: The Buffalo Bills are Jersey bound, heading to East Rutherford to take on the New York Jets this week. It’s just the second divisional game for the Bills, as they have just their October loss vs. the New England Patriots on their AFC East ledger so far. The Jets, meanwhile, will finish their first go-rounds […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are Jersey bound, heading to East Rutherford to take on the New York Jets this week. It’s just the second divisional game for the Bills, as they have just their October loss vs. the New England Patriots on their AFC East ledger so far. The Jets, meanwhile, will finish their first go-rounds of AFC East games with Sunday’s matchup. While New York may be just 2-7 this season, they’ve played a lot of tight games, including two against the New England Patriots and Miami Dolphins. The Patriots defeated the Jets 26-19, while the Dolphins squeaked out a 28-25 victory. Really, the only game the Jets were entirely demolished in came last week, when they lost 35-12 against the Kansas City Chiefs. Can the Jets play the Bills tight this week? Will Buffalo overlook their division rivals and lose the game outright? There’s no question that Buffalo is the better football team, but there’s a reason why they play the games rather than just talking about them. The Bills will need to come out ready to roll in order to maintain their hold on the No. 1 seed in the AFC. Here are five Bills to watch on Sunday as they try to do just that. _____________________________________________________________________________ QB Josh Allen Last week, after a slow start, Allen caught fire in the second half against an outstanding Minnesota Vikings defense. Allen started his night just 7-of-14 for 51 yards and an interception, but from the Bills’ two-minute drive at the end of the first half until the end of the game, he was electric. Allen completed 14 of his next 21 passes for 183 yards and a touchdown, and while those numbers might sound pedestrian, Allen finished his day as just the second quarterback to eclipse 200 yards passing against the Vikings this season. It was the first time anyone had done it since Jordan Love did it for the Green Bay Packers in Week One. Allen isn’t immune from the occasional stinker, and sometimes, those stinkers come against subpar opponents in the immediate aftermath of a big win. OF Buffalo’s three AFC East foes, Allen also has fewer touchdown passes against the Jets (16) than he does against either the Patriots (25) or Dolphins (42) in his career, and he’s thrown 11 interceptions in 15 games against them. I want to see Allen work just as patiently as he did on Monday night, taking what the Jets’ defense gives him while trusting his teammates to do their part. He doesn’t have to play hero ball this week. He just has to be Josh Allen. RB James Cook III Part of me is watching Cook because I expect him to have a big game, as he averaged 4.53 yards per rush in seven career games against the Jets. However, part of me is also watching how head coach and offensive play-caller Joe Brady manages his workload. Cook carried 31 times on Monday, and coming into a short week, I wouldn’t be surprised to see more of Ray Davis in the backfield this week. Cook still needs his touches, but I wouldn’t be mad if his snap share were dialed back a bit in the interest of saving him for later in the season. Davis and Ty Johnson, who is a former Jet, should see some more work this week. If Cook can slip some big runs early, it could help Buffalo to build the kind of lead where he’s hopefully wearing a baseball cap in the fourth quarter. WR DJ Moore Yeah, we’re going heavy-hitters this week. Moore has looked good since returning from a shoulder injury, but I’m waiting for him to take over a game like he did when he had five catches for 100 yards and a score on opening day. That’s also, perhaps not coincidentally, the only game he’s played this season where he wasn’t banged up in some way. Moore is doing his job, as he has 19 catches fo 285 yards and 2 touchdowns on 32 targets; however, he hasn’t looked like a bona fide No. 1 wideout. Against a struggling Jets squad that has allowed 16 passing touchdowns against just one interception this season, I’d like to see Moore have a bigger day. The Jets rank well in passing yards allowed—they’re No. 4 in passing yards against—but that’s misleading since they’re often trailing and they’re ranked just 26th against the run. A scoring pass from Allen to Moore on the first drive of the game for the Bills would be a nice way to kick off a Sunday. OLB Michael Hoecht Maybe it’s unfair to single him out, as Hoecht hasn’t played more than 41% of the defensive snaps in a game this season, and he’s coming off of Achilles surgery last year. However, he’s been mostly pedestrian when he’s been out there, and he just hasn’t had the burst that he showed in limited action last year. Yes, that’s a byproduct of the injury, as he is just past one calendar year since he tore his Achilles in a win over the Chiefs. But, Hoecht has just 15 tackles to show for his work this season, and half a combined sack of Jared Goff in Week Two is his whole pass-rush output so far. He nearly made a cool play last week when he dove and nearly intercepted a spike. Making a play on Geno Smith and bringing the veteran quarterback to the turf would be nice. If Hoecht can find a groove, given how well Greg Rousseau is playing and the strides that T.J. Parker and Bradley Chubb have made as a duo, it would add another layer to Buffalo’s pass rush as they enter a difficult stretch of schedule. S Amani Hooker It has to be the new guy, right? Hooker was exactly the kind of addition the Bills needed. He’s a rangy safety who isn’t afraid to hit, and it sure doesn’t hurt that he’s the NFL’s current leader in interceptions, either. Hooker has allowed just a 60.2 quarterback rating when he’s the closest player in coverage. That’s significantly better than Buffalo’s two starting safeties last week, Cole Bishop (90.3 passer rating allowed) and Damar Hamlin (106 passer rating allowed). Even if the Bills ease him into the festivities, it’s going to be nice to have a high-end safety in the back of the defense. Sunday is a good time to try him out, as the Jets rank just 22nd in passing yards on the year. I’m excited to see what No. 22 brings to Buffalo’s ever-improving defense.

full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images Panthers safety Zakee Wheatley has been fined $5,626 for a hit on a defenseless player in Carolina’s Week 9 loss to the Denver Broncos. The fine was assessed for a first-and-10 Broncos play with 19 seconds to play in the first quarter of Week 9. Marco Wilson was flagged for taunting on the same play, but Wheatley was not flagged at the time. It’s Wheatley’s second fine of the 2026 season. He was also fined $5,626 for taunting against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 6. No Denver players were fined for any plays in the Panthers’ 26-21 loss in Week 9. The NFL divides up the money it collects from player fines between the NFLPA’s efforts to support retired players, the NFL Foundation, and other nonprofits supporting youth sports, community health initiatives, and player health and safety at all levels of sports. The Panthers will face off against the New Orleans Saints on the road in Week 11.

title: One stat shows how Ben Johnson and the Bears are helping Caleb Williams thrive
summary: As rough as Caleb Williams’ night was against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week, those struggles don’t take away from the incredible progress the Chicago Bears quarterback has made in his third NFL season. And as many of us predicted, the jump in his performance has less to do with an increase in the spectacular […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears warms up before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field, Sunday, November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Todd Rosenberg via Getty Images) | Getty Images As rough as Caleb Williams’ night was against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last week, those struggles don’t take away from the incredible progress the Chicago Bears quarterback has made in his third NFL season. And as many of us predicted, the jump in his performance has less to do with an increase in the spectacular as it does with his growing mastery of the ordinary. A recent ESPN analysis of each NFL team’s report card through the first half of the season highlighted just how much Williams has grown for the Bears in a particularly key stat. “Williams leads the NFL in completion percentage (82.8%) when not pressured. He is ahead of the pace for the highest single-season completion percentage in that situation by a season-qualifying quarterback since ESPN first tracked pressures in 2009,” the article lays out. Naturally, you’d expect Williams and most quarterbacks to play better when they’re not pressured. But comparing Williams to himself over the last few years is pretty mindblowing. His passing grade (84.6), adjusted completion percentage (83.7), and passer rating (106.4) when kept clean are all the highest of his career, according to Pro Football Focus. The adjusted completion percentage, in particular, is wildly better than his first two seasons, highlighting his increased ability to hit the easy stuff. It’s also a credit to his coaching and the protection in front of him. Johnson has been in his bag this season, routinely alternating between opening up the middle of the field, creating quick, simple third-down throws, and using the screen game as an extension of the run game to get the ball into playmakers’ hands. Last week’s four-INT game notwithstanding, Williams has done a masterful job of keeping the ball out of harm’s way and taking what the defense gives him. His offensive line has generally held up its end, too, despite facing a revolving door at left tackle due to injuries. Through six games, the Bears offensive line (according to PFF) has been responsible for relatively few pressures compared to other quarterbacks, and Williams (albeit in a smaller sample size) has only been taken down 14 times this year—tied for 21st in the league. It’s not easy protecting for an average of 3.33 seconds each play—the average amount of time Williams takes before throwing. But they’re collectively making it work. Given how hard the Bucs made things for Williams, the rest of the Bears’ opponents will not doubt try to duplicate Tampa Bay’s game plan and force Williams into tough situations. But as long as he continues to make the right plays, especially when he’s kept clean, he and the Bears will be just fine.

title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Updating the League
summary: With the Chicago Bears on the bye week, it felt like a good time to update anyone who has been following the series of articles on the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. We did a series of articles over the summer that included an introduction, grading the draft, and analyzing each team’s roster (If you […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Ceedee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys celebrates a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Chicago Bears on the bye week, it felt like a good time to update anyone who has been following the series of articles on the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. We did a series of articles over the summer that included an introduction, grading the draft, and analyzing each team’s roster (If you search “Dynasty” in the search bar, all the articles will pop up for you). Let’s take a look at how the league has developed 9 weeks into the season. At the top of the standings is Mason West. We said that Mason was going to contend for a championship this year. The concern was how it was going to look after this year with an aging roster. Does it matter? Mason is undefeated at 9-0 and putting up a monstrous 311 PPG. For reference, scoring over 300 is a huge week; Mason is averaging doing it on a weekly basis. 280 to 299 is an excellent week. 260 to 279 I would call a good week. 240 to 259 is decent. 220 to 239 ain’t great. If you are scoring below 220, it’s a brutal week. If you are below 200, just go ahead and quit. Mason can hit you from multiple directions, whether it’s Patrick Mahomes, a running back trio, or some elite WRs and a solid defense; the key on these teams is having enough talent that if a couple of players have a rough week, you have plenty of players able to pick up the slack. While Mason is 9-0, he has some company. Jeff Berckes also sits at 9-0. Before the season started, JB took a big swing and traded away a pile of draft capital for Bijan Robinson. We thought JB was a playoff team before Bijan; we were worried about his depth. With Bijan, his team is clearly the 2nd best team in the league. He’s scoring around 290 PPG, which is also quite a hefty number. There is still definitely a depth concern with JB’s team, but he’s rolling out Joe Burrow, Bijan Robinson, and JSN. That trio is going to push you towards a lot of victories, which has clearly been the case so far. After the top two, things really start getting cluttered. Lester Wiltfong sits in 3rd place, but he was 6-1 and has currently dropped 2 straight. The other issue for Lester is that, while his record is strong, he’s averaging 249 PPG. That puts him 8th (out of 14 teams) in scoring. Lester’s scoring output would make you think that his record should be closer to 4-5, not 6-3, but he’s pulled out some victories and is a couple more wins away from most likely securing a playoff spot. Lester has a solid defense and a nice running back duo with D’Andre Swift and Jonathan Taylor, but his receivers are just not generating enough points right now. There are three teams tied at 5-4. Adam Hess, Brandon Robinson, and Will Ingalls. Poor Will. One of the few guys in the league who is rebuilding and not trying to win, but somehow he keeps putting up Ws. He’s only averaging 237 per game, which is the 2nd lowest output in the league. Making the playoffs would seem like a great Cinderella season, but Will would almost certainly be outmatched by the likes of JB and Mason, and with the 2027 draft looking pretty strong, Will is definitely going to want a top 3 or 4 pick and not be 9th thanks to an early playoff exit. Adam and Brandon are both roughly where they should be. Their scoring outputs are both in the top half in the league, and they are both just above .500. We expected Brandon to battle for a playoff spot, but we thought Adam had a couple of holes to fill before he was ready to compete, specifically at running back. Before the season, he was trotting out Ashton Jeanty and a hope and a prayer. After a couple of trades, he now runs out Jeanty, Christian McCaffrey, and Bucky Irving. He has some young WRs playing well and a couple of big scorers on defense; this team can definitely make the playoffs and make a deep run. Brandon will most likely make the playoffs thanks to a nice RB duo, a solid defense, and a couple of WRs that can put up points, but his QB room is disastrous. His best QB is Sam Darnold, and what’s more alarming than that is that his 2nd-best QB is probably JJ McCarthy. This team can make the playoffs but would be surprising if it can win a playoff game. Our two hard-luck teams are Redacted and Dan Meehan. Redacted is 4-5, Meehan is 3-6. Both of them hold the 3rd and 4th most points per game in the league, but have been on the unfortunate side of some big opponent outputs. Redacted could use his WRs to start putting up some more points, but the talent is there to make the playoffs. He could flirt with a little roster construction and trade away some depth at certain positions to help out with some weaker ones, but I expect this team to make the playoffs, though they probably don’t have a championship pedigree. Meehan has been frustrated with his bad luck and has made some moves to try and reimagine the roster and see if that can help him for this season and the future. There’s talent on the roster, and a lot of it is pretty young. If he can get some scoring out of his defensive line, the playoffs this season are possible if he can get hot. We do have another pair of 4-5 teams with Quinten Krzysko and Kev H. I think both these teams are in the rebuilding stage and probably not headed for the playoffs this year, but both have decent records at this point. Looking at Q’s roster, he has a lot of pretty good players, but he doesn’t have a lot of top-end talent. He’s going to need to secure some if he’s going to push his team into the top tier of the league. Kev is in a bit of trouble. Due to injuries, his 2 QBs are Daniel Jones and Carson Beck. He has a deeper team, but his starters have similar point totals to his bench. Some of his bigger point scorers are on the injured list, but this is another team that’s lacking in elite point scorers. Kev has been working on restructuring his roster, but I fear he has more to do. Next we have a pair of 3-6 teams that are both in the midst of losing streaks. Myself, I’ve lost three straight, and Ron Luce has been in the wrong column for 4 straight weeks. Ron has a foundation but needs to build out the rest of his team. Lamar Jackson’s injury certainly hasn’t helped, but he has plenty of scorers on defense and Jahmyr Gibbs on offense. But his highest-scoring WR is… KALIF RAYMOND?!? Dear God. I was curious if my team was ready to try and make a playoff push or if it needed another year of adding talent. My running back room was razor thin, and after injuries to RJ Harvey and Jeremiyah Love, there’s nothing left in the cupboard. We are officially a year away from hopefully working our way back into the playoffs. There are two teams bringing up the rear: Jacob Infante, who sits at 2-7. If you read the articles over the summer, Jacob inherited a dumpster fire of a team that had Bijan Robinson and nothing else. A king’s ransom was had, and he traded away Bijan, but he is going to need a couple of years of shrewd drafting to get this team turned around. Last place is pretty stunning with Tyler Volz. Tyler was a solid playoff team last year, and we thought he was going to contend again this year. But he sits at 1-8 in last place. There are quite a few Chargers and Eagles on the roster in key spots, and that’s going to doom you pretty quickly in 2026. It’ll be curious to see if Tyler tries to run it back next year and hope for some better luck, or if he feels he needs to rip it down to the studs. title: 5 biggest needs for Bears in 2027 offseason
summary: Heading into their Week 10 bye week, the Bears find themselves with a favorable 7-2 record and a first-place standing in the loaded NFC North. Even with the slight derailment of Caleb Williams missing three games due to injury, they are firmly positioned as one of the top teams in the NFL entering the second […]
full_text: Heading into their Week 10 bye week, the Bears find themselves with a favorable 7-2 record and a first-place standing in the loaded NFC North. Even with the slight derailment of Caleb Williams missing three games due to injury, they are firmly positioned as one of the top teams in the NFL entering the second half of the season. Since the Bears don’t play a game this weekend, now is as good of a time as any to look towards the future. I’m not in full mock offseason mode yet, especially since a few potential cut candidate veterans still have a lot to prove before I feel comfortable projecting who stays and who goes. But for the most part, we know what their biggest strengths and weaknesses will be heading into the 2027 offseason. I’ll be ranking the Bears’ five biggest needs this offseason are, and I’ll include a few prospects in the 2027 NFL Draft that could be of interest in the second round. Since Chicago traded its first-round pick this year for Jeffery Simmons, highlighting potential Day 2 prospects will make up a lot of our draft coverage in the weeks and months ahead. I’ll include players ranked around the Round 2 range using the PFN Consensus Big Board , and I’ll include my own rankings for each player accordingly. 5. Offensive guard Guard is much more of a long-term need than a short-term one, as Joe Thuney is the reigning Protector of the Year, and Jonah Jackson is playing at an All-Pro level in 2026. However, Thuney is experiencing slight regression; his 75.8 PFN OL Impact grade is a considerable dip from his 91.1 grade last year. He’ll be turning 34 years old in a few days, and if the Bears do well enough in the playoffs, it’s possible he could look to call it a career. Obviously, the ideal scenario sees Thuney stick around in Chicago for at least another season. But the team could eventually use a long-term successor to him along its interior offensive line. I wouldn’t expect the Bears to draft a guard early this year, and they have solid depth with the likes of Luke Newman and Jordan McFadden. That said, it’s a position they could address earlier than people expect if the value is right, or if Thuney chooses to retire this offseason. 2027 draft prospects in Round 2: Austin Siereveld, Ohio State (Consensus: 45; Infante: 59) Cayden Green, Missouri (Consensus: 56; Infante: 58) Carter Smith, Indiana (Consensus: 61; Infante: 34) Evan Tengesdahl, Cincinnati (Consensus: 85; Infante: 139) 4. Linebacker Should the Bears let go of T.J. Edwards this offseason, it would free them $8.5 million in cap space in 2027. Among 78 qualified linebackers, his 66.2 PFN LB Impact grade ranks just No. 72 at the position. They could just slide D’Marco Jackson in his place in the starting lineup next year, but there’s also a chance they could draft a linebacker early. I’d keep an eye on speedier players at the position, as defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has emphasized the importance of speed and mobility on his defense. The 2027 draft lacks the blue-chip talent at linebacker that 2026 had in Sonny Styles and Arvell Reese, but there are a handful of solid Day 2 prospects who could be right up Chicago’s alley. 2027 draft prospects in Round 2: Sammy Brown, Clemson (Consensus: 53; Infante: 40) Tony Rojas, Penn State (Consensus: 78; Infante: 67) Sammy Omosigho, UCLA (Consensus: 124; Infante: 81) Rasheem Biles, Texas (Consensus: 183; Infante: 82) 3. Defensive end All things considered, the Bears’ group of defensive ends has been better than I expected it would be going into 2026. Austin Booker has performed at a high level, Dayo Odeyingbo showed improvement before his injury, and Montez Sweat’s play has gotten better since Chicago traded for Jeffery Simmons. There’s still plenty of long-term uncertainty at the position, however. The Bears will need cap space to work with in the 2027 offseason, and it’s likely that a big move will be made at defensive end to free some up. Sweat’s release would create $21 million in cap space, while Odeyingbo’s release would free up $15 million. It’s unlikely they choose to cut both, but one of them could end up as a cap casualty. At that point, Chicago would need a new edge rusher to pair with the likes of Booker, Shemar Turner, and whichever veteran they choose to keep around. Luckily for them, the 2027 draft is deep with high-floor, powerful edge rushers who fit the physical mold that Allen historically prefers in his hand-in-the-dirt defensive ends. 2027 draft prospects in Round 2: Will Heldt, Clemson (Consensus: 54; Infante: 53) Clev Lubin, Louisville (Consensus: 55; Infante: 66) Kenyatta Jackson Jr., Ohio State (Consensus: 72; Infante: 78) Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon (Consensus: 75; Infante: 64) Jordan Ross, LSU (Consensus: 80; Infante: 73) 2. Defensive tackle The addition of Jeffery Simmons has had a massive impact on the Bears’ defense, and part of why the team was willing to give up two first-round picks for him was the fact that he recently signed an extension with the Titans. As a result, Chicago can hold onto him through 2030. His presence definitely helps the interior defensive line, but that group is otherwise pretty thin. Grady Jarrett projects as a cap casualty with the $13.5 million the Bears would free up by releasing him. Elsewhere, they don’t have a proven long-term option at the position outside of Simmons. The likes of Neville Gallimore, Jordan van den Berg, and Jayden Loving could end up as decent depth pieces, but none of them have proven to be starting-caliber players in the NFL (at least not yet, in the case of the latter two). Adding another interior defensive force should be a priority for the Bears, and there happen to be several defensive tackle prospects I like in the Day 2 range of this 2027 draft class, even though they’ll be missing out on some of the first-round talent. 2027 draft prospects in Round 2: Tavion Gadson, Kentucky (Consensus: 46; Infante: 68) Ahmad Moten, Miami (FL) (Consensus: 47; Infante: 18) Justin Scott, Miami (FL) (Consensus: 49; Infante: 44) Bear Alexander, Oregon (Consensus: 57; Infante: 109) A.J. Holmes Jr., Texas Tech (Consensus: 74; Infante: 32) 1. Cornerback This season has been very exciting for the Bears so far, but the biggest disappointment with this team in 2026 has to be the cornerback room. Malik Muhammad has surpassed expectations as a fourth-round rookie, and Kyler Gordon’s return in the slot has been valuable, but Chicago has otherwise faced rocky play at the position along the perimeter. Jaylon Johnson had a pick-six and shut down the Buccaneers’ offense last Sunday night, but he’s played poorly for most of the season. It’s possible the Simmons addition can help turn his season around, but with the $16 million the Bears would free up by releasing him, Johnson remains on the bubble. Tyrique Stevenson is also an impending free agent, and much like Chicago’s many secondary free agents from the 2026 offseason, it feels unlikely that the team extends him. We’ll see which cornerback prospects actually declare for the 2027 draft, but there’s a lot of good value late in Round 2 or early in Round 3 based on my current evaluations. 2027 draft prospects in Round 2: Vicari Swain, South Carolina (Consensus: 50; Infante: 99) Audavion Collins, Penn State (Consensus: 51; Infante: 48) Jalen Mayo, Houston (Consensus: 65; Infante: 77) Andrew Marshall, Nebraska (Consensus: 50; Infante: 49) Zabien Brown, Alabama (Consensus: 82; Infante: 69) DJ McKinney, Notre Dame (Consensus: 87; Infante: 70)

title: Question of the Day: How far do Bears have to go for you to be satisfied?
summary: The Chicago Bears have hit the bye at 7-2 and are sitting in first place of the gauntlet NFC North. The Bears have a tough second-half schedule but certainly appear to be headed to the playoffs for the second consecutive year. Last season, the Bears won the division, won their first playoff game in 15 […]
full_text: Mike Ditka, Chicago Bears' coach, holds a press conference with the Vince Lombardi Trophy firmly in his grasp after his team wins the Super Bowl. (Photo by Bettmann Archive/Getty Images) The Chicago Bears have hit the bye at 7-2 and are sitting in first place of the gauntlet NFC North. The Bears have a tough second-half schedule but certainly appear to be headed to the playoffs for the second consecutive year. Last season, the Bears won the division, won their first playoff game in 15 years, and they were an eyelash away from reaching the NFC Championship Game. I think 99% of Bears fans, after the sting of the Rams loss wore off, were very pleased with the results of the 2025 season, even if they lost the last game they played. This year, at approximately the midway point in the season, the Bears are at or near the top of everyone’s list of a true Super Bowl contender. With more success comes more expectations. How far do Bears have to go for you to be satisfied with their season? I think as fans, when the team is building something, we want to see them improve upon the previous season. Since there were only four teams that had more postseason success than Chicago, there isn’t a ton of room to improve. That being said, I think Bears fans and NFL media around the country expect the Bears to be better than they were in 2025. Answer: I think the first obvious step is that for any level of satisfaction to be reached, the Bears have to be one of the last four remaining teams in the NFL. That’s a lofty thing to say, but I think it’s fair. I think if the Bears make the playoffs but lose in the Wild Card or Divisional round, there will be plenty of disappointment with the fan base. Yes, fans will be excited that the Bears made the playoffs in back-to-back seasons for the first time since 2005 and 2006, but that won’t be good enough. Even if the Bears win a playoff game in back-to-back seasons, it’ll be the first time they’ve done that since 1984 and 1985, but even then, that won’t be good enough. I think for some fans, reaching the NFC Championship Game will be enough. If the San Francisco 49ers are the 1 seed and the Bears go on the road and lose in that game, there will be a certain level of satisfaction, but I still don’t think that’s enough. I think the Bears need to reach the Super Bowl for me to walk away feeling excited without too much disappointment. Obviously, I want them to win, but if Josh Allen climbs the mountaintop and beats the Bears and wins the Super Bowl, am I going to be freaking out? No, I just think the Bears will be ready to take the next step in 2027. What say you, Bears fans? How far do the Bears have to go this year for you to be content with their season? Is it Super Bowl or bust, like it is for Bill Zimmerman? Is it the Lombardi Trophy? Or is a lower level of success good enough for you? Sound off in the comments below!

title: Bears Week 10 Flashbacks: Concannon’s Bombs, Dent’s Dominance, Vasher’s 108 yards
summary: The Bears may be enjoying their bye week, but the Gridiron Time Machine doesn’t need the week off. Instead of our usual three games, we’re digging a little deeper this week with five memorable Week 10 performances, spanning nearly 60 years of Bears history. 1. 1967, Bears vs. Cardinals: Concannon goes deep, over and over […]
full_text: Chicago Bears Nathan Vasher returns a FG for a TD during a game at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois on November 13, 2005. (Photo by Bill Smith/Getty Images) The Bears may be enjoying their bye week, but the Gridiron Time Machine doesn’t need the week off. Instead of our usual three games, we’re digging a little deeper this week with five memorable Week 10 performances, spanning nearly 60 years of Bears history. 1. 1967, Bears vs. Cardinals: Concannon goes deep, over and over again November 19, 1967 | Bears win 30-3 The 1967 Bears were sitting at 4-5 when the St. Louis Cardinals came to Wrigley Field for Week 10. What followed was one of the more explosive passing performances of the era. Jack Concannon completed only 11 passes, but those completions went for an incredible 336 yards and three touchdowns. Dick Gordon was responsible for most of the damage, catching four passes for 179 yards and two scores. The touchdowns were not exactly short ones either. Concannon connected with Gordon for a 93-yard touchdown early in the second quarter, then found Bob Jones for another 51-yard score. Before halftime arrived, Gordon struck again from 67 yards out. Three touchdown passes. All three from more than 50 yards away. Meanwhile, the Bears defense made sure St. Louis never had much of an opportunity to respond. Chicago intercepted Cardinals quarterbacks seven times, including five picks from Jim Hart alone, while forcing nine turnovers overall. The Cardinals finished with only 230 total yards and never reached the end zone. Chicago cruised to a 30-3 victory behind 461 yards of offense. For a franchise that has not exactly been known for explosive passing attacks, Concannon throwing three touchdown passes of 51 yards or longer feels almost out of place in Bears history. Almost. 2. 1979, Bears vs. Lions: Everybody gets involved November 4, 1979 | Bears win 35-7 The Bears entered Week 10 of the 1979 season sitting at 4-5 and desperately trying to remain in the playoff picture. Detroit turned out to be a pretty good opponent for getting things moving in the right direction. Walter Payton once again carried the offense, rushing for 113 yards and two touchdowns on 22 carries while adding another 53 yards as a receiver. Mike Phipps threw for just 136 yards, but Chicago didn’t need much through the air. The fun really started in the third quarter. With Chicago leading 14-7, Steve Schubert returned a punt 77 yards for a touchdown. Not long afterward, Terry Schmidt intercepted Lions quarterback Jeff Komlo and returned it 20 yards for another score. Suddenly, a seven-point game had become a 28-7 Bears lead. Payton added his second touchdown in the fourth quarter to finish off a 35-7 victory. Chicago did not commit a turnover while forcing five from Detroit, and Payton finished with 166 yards from scrimmage. The win moved the Bears back to .500 at 5-5 and became part of a late-season push that eventually carried Chicago into the playoffs. The recipe probably sounds familiar. Give the ball to Walter Payton, let the defense create mistakes, and sneak in a special teams touchdown while you’re at it. Very Bears. 3. 1984, Bears vs. Raiders: Richard Dent wrecks the defending champs November 4, 1984 | Bears win 17-6 One year before the 1985 Bears defense became immortal, Chicago was already showing the rest of the NFL what was coming. The defending Super Bowl champion Los Angeles Raiders arrived at Soldier Field in Week 10 with a 7-2 record. They left having scored zero touchdowns. Walter Payton handled the offensive workload, rushing 27 times for 111 yards and scoring twice in the first half. His touchdown runs of 18 and eight yards gave Chicago a 14-0 advantage before the defense took care of everything else. And Richard Dent was everywhere. Dent recorded 4.5 sacks, which remains the Bears’ single-game franchise record. Chicago sacked Raiders quarterbacks nine times overall, forced five turnovers and held Los Angeles to just 181 total yards. The Raiders managed only two field goals in a 17-6 Bears victory. It was the first time the defending champions had been held without a touchdown in more than three years. The win moved Chicago to 7-3 and gave the Bears another indication that Buddy Ryan’s defense was developing into something special. We know what happened one year later. But before the Super Bowl Shuffle, the playoff shutouts and the legend of the 1985 defense, Richard Dent and company were already making Sundays miserable for opposing quarterbacks. The defending Super Bowl champions just happened to get an early preview. 4. 1990, Bears vs. Falcons: Vestee Jackson shuts the door November 11, 1990 | Bears win 30-24 The Bears entered Week 10 of the 1990 season as one of the hottest teams in football. Atlanta came to Soldier Field and nearly spoiled the afternoon. After falling behind 3-0, Chicago scored 24 unanswered points behind touchdowns from Neal Anderson, Wendell Davis and Brad Muster. Jim Harbaugh connected with Davis for an eight-yard touchdown in the second quarter, and the Bears carried a 24-3 advantage into the second half. Then things got uncomfortable. Atlanta scored two unanswered touchdowns to cut the lead to 24-17, and what had looked like a comfortable afternoon suddenly became a one-score game. Fortunately, Chris Miller threw one pass too many. Vestee Jackson jumped the route and returned the interception 45 yards for a touchdown, pushing the lead back to 30-17 with just over a minute remaining. Atlanta scored once more, but Chicago held on for a 30-24 victory. Miller threw for 239 yards and two touchdowns, but the Bears intercepted him four times. Wendell Davis led Chicago offensively with five catches for 105 yards and a score, while Harbaugh added 195 passing yards and another 47 on the ground. The victory improved Chicago to 8-1 and extended its winning streak to five games. Sometimes the defense dominates from start to finish. Other times it waits until things get interesting before reminding everyone who is in charge. 5. 2005, Bears vs. 49ers: Nathan Vasher goes 108 yards November 13, 2005 | Bears win 17-9 If you remember anything about the Bears’ 2005 Week 10 win over San Francisco, it probably isn’t the offense. That’s because there wasn’t much of one. Chicago quarterback Kyle Orton threw for only 67 yards. San Francisco quarterback Cody Pickett somehow managed just one completion for 28 yards. The real star was the wind. With gusts approaching 50 miles per hour at Soldier Field, 49ers kicker Joe Nedney attempted a 52-yard field goal on the final play of the first half. The kick fell short. Nathan Vasher was waiting. Vasher caught the ball deep in the end zone, briefly hesitated, then took off. He reversed field, found a convoy of blockers and raced all the way to the opposite end zone for a 108-yard touchdown. At the time, it was the longest play in NFL history. The return gave Chicago a 7-3 halftime lead in a game where points were extremely difficult to find. Adrian Peterson later rushed for a seven-yard touchdown and finished with 120 yards on 24 carries, while Robbie Gould added a fourth-quarter field goal. The Bears held on for a 17-9 victory, their fifth straight win, improving to 6-3 while maintaining control of the NFC North. One year later, Devin Hester would return another missed field goal exactly 108 yards against the Giants. Apparently 108-yard missed field goal returns were just something Bears defensive backs did for a while. Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs .

title: Bengals could end up with more egg on their face from Arnold Ebiketie trade debacle
summary: The NFL’s system to decide who gets compensatory draft picks is complicated, and that’s an understatement. As it stands right now, the Cincinnati Bengals will receive an extra third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft due to the free agency loss of Trey Hendrickson to the Ravens. And that’s one of the reasons the Bengals […]
full_text: The NFL’s system to decide who gets compensatory draft picks is complicated, and that’s an understatement. As it stands right now, the Cincinnati Bengals will receive an extra third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft due to the free agency loss of Trey Hendrickson to the Ravens. And that’s one of the reasons the Bengals ended up backing out of their trade with the Eagles for edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie on Tuesday before the deadline came at 4 PM. The Bengals, a little before noon, agreed to send a sixth-round pick to the Eagles in exchange for Ebiketie, but after OverTheCap.com’s Nick Korte pointed that the Bengals could lose their compensatory pick in the trade went through, the Bengals backed out. A press conference in which the head coach apologized on behalf of the de facto GM later, and the entire team had a decent amount of egg on their face. The Bengals agreed to the Arnold Ebiketie trade before asking the NFL how it’d affect them in the complex compensatory pick formula — a mistake for which Duke Tobin apologized to the Eagles as he called off the deal. More in The Sweep: https://t.co/rSR29qle6s pic.twitter.com/UYrSp36teo — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) November 14, 2026 And now it gets worse (maybe). The Seattle Seahawks signed former Bengals guard Cordell Volson to their practice squad. If he were to make the active roster and play enough snaps as a starter for the Seahawks, he could, potentially, count as a compensatory free agent, which could give the Bengals an extra seventh-round pick and have allowed that Ebiketie trade to go through without sacrificing the third-round compensatory pick. Again, this is a big “what if” scenario, and I can’t even pretend I know the ins and outs of the compensatory system (there are few that do… especially inside the offices of Paycor Stadium), but wouldn’t it just seem to work out that way for the Bengals? If Volson somehow becomes a starter he could end up counting as a compensatory free agent (maybe, since it's a different team from his original signing and the CBA isn't clear about this) and get the Bengals an extra 7th And would have potentially allowed the Ebiketie trade lol https://t.co/VV6GKu94Aq — Jake Liscow (@JakeLiscow) November 12, 2026

title: Bengals vs. Steelers on SNF carries special meaning for Orlando Brown Jr.
summary: Cincinnati Bengals starting left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. isn’t about to pretend this is just another game. Not with the Pittsburgh Steelers coming to town with first place in the AFC North on the line. Asked whether Sunday’s showdown means more to the Bengals than any other game right now, Brown gave the answer fans […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals starting left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. isn’t about to pretend this is just another game. Not with the Pittsburgh Steelers coming to town with first place in the AFC North on the line. Asked whether Sunday’s showdown means more to the Bengals than any other game right now, Brown gave the answer fans probably wanted to hear. “Hell yeah,” Brown said in a video recently. "I usually don't say this, but I would tell you, hell yeah." Orlando Brown Jr. on if this game means more to the #Bengals right now than any other game. @FOX19 pic.twitter.com/GpZ8Nu6kEa — Jeremy Rauch (@FOX19Jeremy) November 11, 2026 Both teams enter Sunday night’s matchup at Paycor Stadium with 6-2 records. Kickoff is scheduled for 8:20 p.m. ET on NBC, giving the Bengals a national stage and a home crowd for a game with immediate consequences atop the division. For Brown, the opportunity extends beyond the players taking the field. He wants Cincinnati’s fans to experience the kind of meaningful football that makes a stadium feel different from kickoff to final gun. “I’m really excited for the City of Cincinnati,” Brown said. “Our fans deserve the opportunity to be able to pay to go to games like this and to be able to suit up in front of them with everything at stake on Sunday, and I’m looking forward to it.” That is a welcome departure from the familiar insistence that every opponent presents the same challenge, and every Sunday carries the same weight. Players can prepare with the same discipline each week while acknowledging that some games simply mean more. “I feel like we play with a chip on our shoulder for a lot of different reasons, but to tell you that this game means more to us, I normally don’t say this, but I would say, ‘hell yeah,’” Brown said. Brown’s challenge now is to help turn those words into the protection Joe Burrow needs. The Bengals will need their left tackle, along with the rest of the offensive line, to give the offense time to operate. Enthusiasm matters, but execution will decide whether Cincinnati ends the night celebrating. An unnecessary penalty, a missed assignment, or a stalled possession can quickly overwhelm whatever energy a team brings out of the tunnel. Still, there is something refreshing about hearing a veteran acknowledge the moment without trying to shrink from it. Brown understands the opponent, the opportunity, and what a win would mean to the people filling the stands.

full_text: The expectations for the Cleveland Browns were fairly mixed coming into the season. There was a lot of optimism surrounding the young talent on the roster, but there were still many questions about the quarterback position and what the team would be able to accomplish offensively. There have been plenty of ups and downs this season, along with a lot of inconsistency, but a few areas have been particularly disappointing. The inconsistency on offense definitely tops the list of disappointments this season. From one week to the next, it is tough to know what version of the offense will show up. The offensive line, in particular, has had some good moments, but it has consistently struggled to protect the quarterback and has made it difficult for the run game to get going. This has made it difficult for the offense to perform at a high level. Costly mistakes have been another big issue for this team, as they lead the league in penalties this season with 82 . This comes out to 9.1 penalties per game. These costly mistakes put the offense in difficult yardage situations and make it harder to move the ball down the field. Especially in close games, a few penalties can really make the difference between winning and losing. The biggest question for the Browns, starting today in Week 10, is whether they can turn the disappointments around and how quickly. The Browns are 4.5-point underdogs against the Texans, according to FanDuel Sportsbook . Last week was the second time this season that we didn’t hit on any of our picks. RB Quinshon Judkins didn’t get it going in the running game like I expected, TE Harold Fannin came up two yards short of what he needed, and Isaiah Bond didn’t even have an offensive snap, let alone a receiving touchdown. Let’s do better this week. Here are my favorite player prop bets from the Browns’ perspective in Week 10. Browns vs. Texans NFL player prop bets Dylan Sampson Over 22.5 Receiving Yards (-113) This bet has worked (or would have worked) three weeks in a row, so why not keep riding the gravy train? The bonus here is that the Browns often utilize Dylan Sampson , and Deshaun Watson isn’t wanting to force balls, so Sampson will always get some looks that way. And then, in two-minute situations, or if the team is behind later, Sampson is also the guy in the game to catch passes. The Jaguars’ pass defense is susceptible, so take Sampson again here. Denzel Boston Over 45.5 Receiving Yards (-113) After somewhat of a three-week lull in receiving yards, Denzel Boston had a season-high 98 yards receiving last week. Houston’s defense has been prone to giving up the big passing plays, so this could be another week if Boston catching a long ball and getting all of this yardage in one moment. I’m expecting that Cleveland won’t be able to run the ball effectively, so they should have a gameplan to come out aggressive in the passing game. Deshaun Watson Over 208.5 Passing Yards (-113) If you believe the theme that I’m saying — Cleveland won’t be able to run the ball, but they’ll get the passing yards against this Texans defense — then Deshaun Watson throwing for 209+ yards seems feasible. For some perspective, the Browns are allowing 201 yards passing (6th in the NFL) per game, while the Texans are allowing 236 yards passing (27th in NFL). I don’t have a parlay listed here, but if you’re going to attempt a parlay, all three of the picks in this article — along with a Browns win (might as well go big with a parlay) — would be something you could try. title: NFL predictions: In Browns-Texans, Cleveland needs to turn the corner to become a serious threat
summary: This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-4) take on the Houston Texans (3-5). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game. Time to Show Something Different The start to the season for the Cleveland Browns was a feel-good story. Todd Monken in […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Todd Monken of the Cleveland Browns tips his cap prior to a game against the Baltimore Ravens at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-4) take on the Houston Texans (3-5). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game. Time to Show Something Different The start to the season for the Cleveland Browns was a feel-good story. Todd Monken in his first year as a head coach, all of the young players shining at times, and Deshaun Watson having five game-winning drives. And it was fun to harp on the incredible stat of all of those victories having game-winning drives, but we all know that isn’t sustainable. If the Browns want to contend for the postseason the rest of the year, something has to change. The penalties haven’t gone away. The slow starts haven’t gone away. Playing every winnable game down-to-the-wire hasn’t gone away. The run game issues on both sides haven’t gone away. I praised Todd Monken and Mike Rutenberg earlier this season for their ability to adapt and make adjustments. I don’t think that has stalled, I think what we’re seeing now are the true weaknesses of this team, and they aren’t marks of a playoff contender. Cleveland’s hopes seem to rest on taking advantage of their easy schedule, but they’ve blown their margin for error in that category too with losses to the Jets and Saints. I think the coaching staff is trying to get it fixed each week, but so far they’ve mostly come up empty. That doesn’t mean the team can’t turn the corner in some of those areas, but the thing I keep saying now is, “this is the team’s four-game home stretch.” I don’t necessarily expect them to win all four games, which would put them at a ridiculous 7-0 at home, but on a game-by-game basis, we need to see this team pull of a dominant performance somewhere. Something to further bolster their confidence, further establish their identity, and to ride for the rest of the season. The X-Factor As a follow-up to the above, there is one X-factor who could, at any point, make a monumental difference to the team. Let’s get into it with some of our miscellaneous notes this week: That X-factor would be……….DE Jared Verse . It’s been a storyline all season — he was brought here, not to replicate what Myles Garrett did, but to be a damn-good alternative to him, at least when it comes to pressuring the quarterback. Overall, despite the run defense woes, the Browns’ defense has been fairly solid this season, and the sacks are coming from everywhere but the edge. If Cleveland’s defense is doing this good with Verse being a non-factor, or dare I say it, a liability, what is the upside to this unit if the switch finally flips for him? We’ve hated on Verse a lot, but this week, he finally admitted that he hasn’t played to the standard he wants, and that he’s talked to the team’s psychiatrist about it. I’m a firm believer in how the mental aspects of things can screw with your game. We see it most obviously with kickers all the time. Sometimes we see it with receivers and their drops. I thought Deshaun Watson had a mental block the past several years that he finally seems to have cleared. It’s possible it’s there with Verse. Verse says it’s not physical, so something has to explain the extreme dropoff of being one of the league’s best to one of the league’s worst performing players. Maybe this is a step to somewhat tackling whatever is getting in the way of him being the player he’s proven he can be. If he can deliver that against the Texans, maybe it’s the boost that Cleveland needs to put away a game. That presents us with the unique challenge of trying to figure out which Houston Texans team we’ll see. C.J. Stroud has been a bit of a disappointment the past few years, and last year, the team went on an incredible stretch to close out the year due to their defense. This season, I feel like the defense has been crap, and Stroud is lighting it up most weeks. But this defense should be better; they’ve often been plagued by giving up big plays in pass defense. Cleveland’s pass defense needs to be up to the challenge this week. Although some teams have used the run lately to combat the Browns, I feel like Houston won’t be so committed to the ground game. Deshaun Watson starting over Shedeur Sanders this week is probably the right call. As much as I enjoyed Sanders finally letting loose in the fourth quarter and overtime last week, many of those plays aren’t sustainable. When it was time to read-and-react in the first several quarters, things were too slow still, the operation was off, etc. The offense has had similar slow starts with Watson, of course, but the operation for the most part has been smooth with him. According to FanDuel , the Browns are 4.5 point underdogs against the Texans. The over/under is 40.5. Quick Hitters Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer talked about how the team has tried to work on ways to start faster offensively: “Yeah, the first thing as a staff, we looked at everything that we’ve done early in games, and when we looked at it, it was like, man, we’ve kind of tried a little bit of everything as far as, hey, let’s maybe call some can plays early, or we’ve tried running it early. We’ve tried movement passes. So, we looked at that, and nothing really spiked out as far as, hey, this is the direction we should go there. And then we’ve also just stressed it to the guys, especially early in practice, like Wednesdays, the first period is always a tempo period, the first team period, so we’ve tried to stress it there. It’s like, okay, we’re going fast, but also, hey, we’re trying to start fast. That’s the point of this period here. And yeah, I can’t say that it’s been like one thing that jumped out to us. We just got to keep attacking it and try to stress it and just try to get better there.” Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg was asked about Jared Verse’s admission that he’s seen the team psychiatrist to try to be a better pass rusher: “I’m not going to discuss Jared Verse in terms of what he does off the field, but I’m really proud of Jared for his approach, for his attitude, the way he’s working with his teammates and our D-line coaching staff to help himself get to where he wants to go.” Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about gunners when they run out of bounds (as Cleveland did last week): “All right, so when you’re putting the ball, you’re putting it toward – usually you’re trying to punt it toward the boundary to shorten the field. And so, you have releases by the gunners toward the punt direction. So, you’d like for both your gunners to release the same direction. So, if you’re punting left, both guys release left, and one guy ends up into the boundary. Now, you can’t run out of bounds on your own. A lot of times those corners will force you into the white. And so now you have to, take a line to re-enter. You know, what happened on that play was, DT (Daniel Thomas) didn’t realize he had gotten in the white, and so we just had a discussion on the sideline and just said, ‘hey, if there’s any possibility that you could have gone out of bounds, all you got to do is just point to the ball, tell your teammates, you, you, you, and they touch it.’ So, it’s a big learning experience for us, and unfortunately, it cost us 30 yards of field position, so we had to learn the hard way. But I just don’t think that it’s possible to change what we do in terms of staying out of bounds. That’s just part of the deal.” Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN: Predictions Chris Pokorny: “The Browns have played a lot of close games, and are 3-0 at home, so this four-game home stretch that they are beginning is vital for them to stay in the playoff race. full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns made a series of roster moves on Saturday as they prepare for their Week 10 game against the Houston Texans. Cleveland added a pair of tight ends as they signed Carsen Ryan to the active roster and elevated Zaire Mitchell-Paden from the practice squad. The club also placed fullback Michael Burton on the injured reserve list with a calf injury, meaning he will miss the next four games. The 6-foot-3 and 255-pound Ryan was selected by the Browns in the seventh round of this year’s NFL Draft. He was released on October 26, re-signed two days later to the practice squad, waived on November 7, only to rejoin the practice squad two days later. Between all that, Ryan has appeared in eight games, primarily on special teams (109 snaps), as he has only seen two snaps on offense. The 6-foot-5 and 257-pound Mitchell-Paden was just signed to Cleveland’s practice squad on Wednesday . He originally signed with the Browns as an undrafted free agent back in 2022. He spent two seasons on Cleveland’s practice squad (2022 and 2023), and split the 2025 season between the Baltimore Ravens (six games, one reception for three yards) and the New Orleans Saints (two games, one reception for 14 yards). Burton is in his first season with the Browns after signing with the team in free agency. With Cleveland, he has appeared in nine games, making two starts, and has been utilized as a blocker while also seeing snaps on special teams. We have activated Jake Hummel to the active roster and made other roster moves. pic.twitter.com/gYrBdSgeXG — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) November 14, 2026 For the Texans, running back David Montgomery, who was questionable with a groin injury, and cornerback Jaylin Smith, who was questionable with a hamstring injury, are not traveling to Cleveland and have been ruled out for the game. In addition, offensive tackle Braden Smith is now questionable as he is dealing with an illness. To fill out their game-day roster, the Texans activated linebacker Jake Hummel, and elevated linebacker Chad Muma and running back Dare Ogunbowale from the practice squad. full_text: Each week for our Browns Reacts results, we have been showing you the fan confidence meter with respect to the direction of the team. This week, we’re also showing the season-wide progress of that fan confidence, so you can see how it has fluctuated amidst the team’s 5-4 record. After the team’s opening loss to the Jaguars, the confidence rightfully tanked, as fans wondered if this team could even win a game this year. Then, the script flipped after the win against the Buccaneers in Week 3, and the momentum continued to build as Deshaun Watson performed better than expected. Things were at a high near when Cleveland defeated their division-rival Baltimore Ravens (after already having beaten the Steelers). However, things are on shakier ground now that Cleveland has lost back-to-back games for the first time this season (to Pittsburgh and New Orleans). As noted above and below, the Browns’ fan confidence took another hit this week, although not a substantial one. Week-to-week, fan confidence decreased by 3 percentage points down to 57%. We are nearing a breaking point, though, since Cleveland has to capitalize on this upcoming four-game home stretch that they gave. By comparison, 24% of Texans fans are confident in the direction of their team. Browns fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app! Take Reacts surveys, create Browns polls, and see how your answers compare with fellow Dawgs By Nature fans. Then discuss the results with the Dawg Pound. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Besides the confidence meter, the main question we asked this week was who should (or should have) started at quarterback against the Texans: Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders . We know that Todd Monken is starting Watson, but we still wanted to gauge what fans preferred heading into the game, after last week’s situation. 59% of fans cast their vote for Watson, while 41% said Sanders. That’s something to keep in mind regarding fan sentiment if Watson struggles during this upcoming four-game home stretch. Here’s what one fan who voted for Watson said: At this point a playoff spot is in the picture, you have to start the guy who gives you the best chance to win. Easily Watson at this point; he’s not great, but he operates the offense better than Shedeur does on a down-to-down basis. Shedeur probably gives you more splash plays (in either direction) so if we need variance, that’s the way I’d go, but I don’t think this schedule demands variance; I think it needs more consistency. According to FanDuel , the Browns are 4.5 point underdogs against the Texans this week, with the over/under being 40.5.

summary: The Cleveland Browns host the Houston Texans on Sunday in a game with actual playoff implications for both teams. full_text: (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) The Cleveland Browns host the Houston Texans on Sunday in a game with actual playoff implications for both teams . Cleveland is currently tied with the New England Patriots for the final playoff spot in the AFC, but the Patriots hold the edge with a 5-1 record in the conference. The Browns already have three conference losses, so a fourth one on Sunday would put a major dent in their playoff hopes and also give the Texans the tiebreaker. But if the Browns pick up the win? Then they will enter the bye week with a 45 percent chance of making the playoffs, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator , which means meaningful football will be on the docket for the rest of the season. While much of the focus of Sunday’s game will be on how Cleveland’s offensive line can keep Houston’s pass rush, which comes into the game tied for first in the league with 29 sacks, away from quarterback Deshaun Watson, who has taken a league-high 33 sacks, there are other matchups to watch. Here are two in particular to keep an eye on, according to Pro Football Focus. Houston WR Nico Collins vs. Cleveland CB Denzel Ward Collins is second on the Texans in receptions (28), and first in receiving yards (384) and receiving touchdowns (4). But he hasn’t had an explosive game since early October when he torched the Dallas Cowboys with seven receptions for 118 yards and two touchdowns. Ward, meanwhile, is putting together his standard season of high-level play, which makes for a good matchup, according to PFF : Collins has missed time in 2026 but has been tremendously dynamic as usual when healthy. He’s notched an 82.8 PFF receiving grade along with 2.10 yards per route run, with 2026 marking his fourth straight season with numbers reaching those thresholds. Further, Collins’ 82.4% contested catch rate is the third-best among receivers with 35 or more targets. Ward has starred from the outset this season, earning a 72.0-plus PFF coverage grade in all but one game throughout the year. He’s permitted just 18 catches for 129 yards across 349 coverage snaps, numbers that warrant being a first-team All-Pro through the midway point of 2026. These two standouts haven’t gone head-to-head in a game since the 2023 postseason, although Ward has generally had Collins’ number. Collins has been held to two catches for 53 yards over their three games facing one another, with Ward winning 75% of the reps in terms of being charted as open. Cleveland WR Denzel Boston vs. Houston CB Derek Stingley Jr. Boston came close to his first 100-yard receiving day last week against the New Orleans Saints (six receptions for 98 yards), and leads all rookies in receiving yards (507). Stingley is currently going through a down year, so if Boston can play through his toe injury, this could be an area for the Browns to exploit, according to PFF : Collins vs. Ward is the meeting of two longtime great players, but Boston vs. Stingley represents the next generation of potential showstopping receiver-corner battles. Boston looks like the frontrunner for Offensive Rookie of the Year through the season’s midway point. He’s collected a 70.3 PFF receiving grade while averaging 1.55 yards per route run. Likewise, Boston’s 5.0 yards after the catch per reception sit in the 74th percentile. Like the rest of Houston’s regressing defense, Stingley has had some trouble this season — producing a career-low 65.3 PFF receiving grade with a 92.4 passer rating allowed. Although the All-Pro has let up 65-plus yards in three separate games, he’s also broken up five passes. Boston has dealt with a toe injury in practice but indicated he expects to play on Sunday. That means we should be treated to a physical showdown between the big-frame rookie and one of the game’s top defensive backs over the last few seasons. The Browns have an opportunity on Sunday to go into their bye week on a positive note and come out on the other side with a legitimate chance to stay in the playoff race. title: FAA ground stop could impact Browns vs. Texans, rest of Week 10 in a big way
summary: When it comes to things of importance, sports might be much lower on the totem pole than many of us devoted fans realize or even think about. Friday’s FAA ground stop to all outgoing flights was an example of a real-world issue impacting many people in many ways, but it could also impact the world […]
full_text: When it comes to things of importance, sports might be much lower on the totem pole than many of us devoted fans realize or even think about. Friday’s FAA ground stop to all outgoing flights was an example of a real-world issue impacting many people in many ways, but it could also impact the world of sports. Many college games on Saturday were still up in the air late Friday night into Saturday morning due to the grounding. As flights got back going after 9 PM on Friday, how airlines and systems would prioritize the restart was something important to watch. “Smaller movements will take a lower priority,” with football teams encouraged to contact the FAA to try to get their flights scheduled. The Houston Texans are still in Texas early Saturday morning. While there is unlikely to be an issue with them getting to Cleveland to face the Browns, it is possible that their schedule will be impacted, including the team’s normal Saturday walkthrough. That will likely be true for all visiting teams this week. The bigger impact on the field could come from the officials for the game. Unlike teams, referees do not travel on a specific charter that can be organized with the FAA. College officials have already raised concerns about their officials making it to their destinations: The numbers are staggering : 12,506 flights have been cancelled so far between yesterday and today, per Flight Aware. The number is expected to grow throughout the day. On Saturday morning already, 3,374 flights have been canceled and 1,008 are delayed nationwide, per FlightAware. In the NFL, like college, refs generally have full-time jobs doing other things throughout the week, and most are scheduled to work most or every weekend. While the NFL generally has backup plans, getting enough officials to their right spots might be tough given the above numbers. Visiting teams could be impacted by the FAA ground stop, but all games could see an impact in how many officials are assigned and in what position those officials are assigned on Sunday. Something for fans to remember if/when a big call does or doesn’t go the Browns’ way.
