title: Chiefs-Falcons: 5 Things to Watch in Week 10 matchup
summary: It’s hard to believe Week 10 is here already, but time flies in the NFL! The Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) will play the Atlanta Falcons (3-6) on the road this week in an interconference duel. The game kicks off at noon Arrowhead time from Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta and will be broadcast on CBS. The […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s hard to believe Week 10 is here already, but time flies in the NFL! The Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) will play the Atlanta Falcons (3-6) on the road this week in an interconference duel. The game kicks off at noon Arrowhead time from Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta and will be broadcast on CBS . The Chiefs defeated the New York Jets last week 35-12 in a blowout at Arrowhead Stadium. During the week, the Chiefs traded for wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts , who will likely make his debut on Sunday. The Atlanta Falcons were defeated 34-17 by the Cincinnati Bengals at home last week, falling to last place in the NFC South. During the week, the Falcons traded All-Pro safety Jessie Bates to the Jacksonville Jaguars in exchange for draft picks. These teams are on opposite ends of the competitiveness spectrum, but they still have to tee it up on Sunday. Here are five things to watch : 1. Josh Downs’ Chiefs debut A former third-round pick out of North Carolina, Downs has accumulated 2,494 yards and 12 touchdowns through his career. At 5 feet 9 inches tall and 171 pounds, Downs relies on quick feet and good route running to win snaps against one-on-one coverage. Since Tyquan Thornton’s ankle dislocation in Week 4 against the Las Vegas Raiders , the Chiefs haven’t found a player who can stretch the field deep and take the top off the defense. Downs has the speed and ball-tracking ability to fill this role. It will be interesting to see how the Chiefs plan to use him this week, but I would expect them to get him involved early and often. Josh Downs 91.0 grade vs Man Coverage 1.71 Seperation Score 34.0 % First Read Target Share vs Man T10 in yards vs Man this year pic.twitter.com/Iwh115QDRl — #babyglitch (@Cxmxthzine) November 10, 2026 2. Who is the punt returner ? The corresponding move to the Downs trade was releasing return man Nikko Remigio. Many thought Remigio would make it back to the practice squad, but a day later the Houston Texans signed him, effectively ending his four-year tenure in Kansas City. Beyond his ability to return punts and kicks, Remigio provided little value to the Chiefs’ offense, but special teams coordinator Dave Toub suggested the team could turn to its crop of young offensive talent to take over the return game during his press conference on Thursday. Coach Toub mentions Josh Downs, Xavier Worthy, Cyrus Allen and Emmett Johnson as options at punt returner moving forward. — Matt McMullen (@KCChiefs_Matt) November 12, 2026 Johnson and Allen have both had shots at returning kickoffs this season, while Worthy has yet to return a kickoff and has returned only one punt. Among the players mentioned by Toub, Downs has the most experience returning punts, with 32 career returns through four seasons. “He’s got 80 reps back there as a punt returner in his career since 2023,” Toub said. “So he’s lined up back there a lot. He’s a good catcher. I went through every one of them. He’s dynamic at times when he gets out. Here's a quick look at new Chiefs' WR Josh Downs at today's practice. Participated in the WR and punt return drills during the media viewing portion of practice. #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/CD330TXhgB — Mark Poulose (@MarkPoulose) November 12, 2026 While Remigio was often reliable and secure with the ball, his lack of involvement elsewhere on the team likely led to his release, as the Chiefs also needed to give younger players chances to get involved. Hopefully, this decision wasn’t made without careful consideration, because punt-return snafus can decide football games. 3. Stopping Bijan Robinson This week, the Chiefs will face the task of stopping the league’s leading rusher, Bijan Robinson. With 880 rushing yards so far this season, five touchdowns, and an average of 5.2 yards per carry — fourth in the NFL — the Falcons’ running back is on pace for well over 1,000 yards for the third straight season. Robinson could be a leading candidate for NFL Offensive Player of the Year — in competition with Kenneth Walker — so the front seven will need to bring their A-game this week. As it stands, the Chiefs defense ranks seventh in the NFL in rushing yards allowed, with only 780 total and 3.6 yards per carry, tied for fifth in the league. Last week, the Chiefs defense gave up some pops early to the Jets’ Braelon Allen and Breece Hall, but locked in in the second half. Bijan Robinson reached a top speed of 21.78 mph on his 59-yard TD run, the second-fastest speed by a ball carrier this season and the second-fastest of Robinson's career. @ATLvsNO | #DirtyBirds pic.twitter.com/Id3snQvOyv — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) October 6, 2026 This week, the focus will need to be there from the jump, because one wrong move or one slow read and Robinson could be off to the races. 4. Turnover differential This week, the Chiefs will carry a +4 turnover differential, tied for 9th in the NFL. The Falcons are on the opposite end, sitting at a -8 margin, tied for 30th in the league. The Falcons have forced only 9 takeaways so far this season, but have thrown a whopping 12 interceptions — most in the league by a team — and lost five fumbles. FOUR quarterbacks have thrown interceptions this season in Atlanta, with Michael Penix throwing six, with backups Cooper Rush(4), Jack Strand (1), and Tua Tagovailoa(1) contributing as well. Michael Penix Jr. É INTERCEPTADO no final do último quarto! 😱 📺: #CINvsATL – ao vivo no SporTV2 e GE TV pic.twitter.com/wl4EEQc4Ps — NFL Brasil (@NFLBrasil) November 8, 2026 The turnover issues in Atlanta have fallen on their quarterbacks’ shoulders, and their defense hasn’t been able to make up for it. The Chiefs have forced five fumbles and intercepted six passes this year, but offensive efficiency with the ball has been the key. They lead the league in ball security and should be able to do so against the Falcons. 5. Harrison Butker (again) Any other kicker in the NFL would be released by now and planning a post-football career. However, when you have made as many big kicks as Harrison Butker has in his career, leeway is due in the eyes of the Chiefs coaching staff, even if his performance and production aren’t. Harrison Butker misses back-to-back attempts in similar fashion following a penalty. Chiefs fans boo loudly as they head to halftime pic.twitter.com/F1BfHbIiPT — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) November 8, 2026 The Chiefs’ long-time kicker missed back-to-back kicks last week, dropping to only 63% for the season, and was showered with jeers by the Arrowhead faithful. This week, Andy Reid and Dave Toub once again stuck with the three-time Super Bowl winner. “He’s going to come through it,” Toub said on Thursday. “I mean, we’re confident that he will. We’re just going to keep practicing him and keep working on little things, and he’s looked good in practice. There’s a reason why he’s still our kicker.” Butker is an Atlanta native and will be kicking in his hometown this week. While he will likely have support in the stands and from the coaching staff, he must perform on the field, or it should be the end of an era in Kansas City.

Each week, we send out questions to the most plugged-in Kansas City Chiefs fans. You can see all of the recent survey results here . And be sure to check out FanDuel Sportsbook , the official sportsbook partner of SB Nation. Chiefs fans’ confidence That’s up 22% from a week ago, when we ran the same poll. I guess beating a bad team does that for you. Nothing instills confidence in a team like your team bullying a lesser opponent and stealing their lunch money, which the Chiefs gladly did to the New York Jets last week. The Chiefs have another chance to rebuild fans’ confidence in the team this Sunday when they take on the hapless Atlanta Falcons . We’ll see how quickly new addition wide receiver Josh Downs can get in the mix and start making his presence felt on the field. If so, we may continue to see the fans’ confidence rise if Kansas City can go on a winning streak. Regardless. As long as we can keep winning games, I suspect this confidence number will grow right along with it. Can the Chiefs still win the division? While it’s nowhere near the realm of possibility that Denver drops a couple of games in the coming weeks, their next five games are not exactly a murderer’s row of competition. The Denver Broncos play the Las Vegas Raiders twice, and the New York Jets , the Pittsburgh Steelers , and the Miami Dolphins each once. The Steelers are the one game where I think the other team could give Denver a run for its money. And I have to admit that it feels a little dirty to be in the awkward position of cheering on the Raiders this weekend. But here we are. I have to admit that 50% also feels about right as to whether the Chiefs can win this division. They are by no means a perfect team, but they are good enough that they could win any game they are a part of, and if a team like that gets on a roll, they can be very dangerous. title: Two of these NFC teams with winning records will miss playoffs
summary: At the NFL season midpoint, the NFC playoff picture is in clear focus. The NFC East and NFC South divisions will send their first place teams to the postseason and they will play host in the opening round. At this point, it feels very unlikely either of them will have a wildcard entrant. That means […]
full_text: At the NFL season midpoint, the NFC playoff picture is in clear focus. The NFC East and NFC South divisions will send their first place teams to the postseason and they will play host in the opening round. At this point, it feels very unlikely either of them will have a wildcard entrant. That means the NFC West and NFC North are directly competing for the three spots left open for non-divisional winners. Out of these seven teams with winning records , two will be watching the playoffs from their couch: The San Francisco 49ers are on their way to winning the West, and we have very little to point to the contrary. The winning of the North will likely come down to the wire. That leaves the remaining three teams from the north against the Los Angeles Rams and Seahawks in the standings. The Chicago Bears close their season with three divisional games, which means they are the most in control of their destiny. The Rams and Seahawks will see each other in two of the final three weeks of the year. The worst case for these teams is that the outcomes are split—which could make them both a victim to the north. If one of these rivals take both games, they likely make the playoffs while the other watches from home. Another key upcoming game for the Rams comes out of their bye week when they host the Green Bay Packers on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Davante Adams seems slated to return against his former team. This is also the targeted return for EDGE rusher Micah Parsons. The forces working against the Rams is the fact they have (by far) the toughest remaining strength of schedule and their roster is not at full force—especially on offense. The eventual returns of Puka Nacua and Terrance Ferguson should bolster the group, but LA must remain in the hunt to buy them enough time. Things are about to get very interesting in the NFC playoff picture. The backhalf of the season will be littered with contests that carry outsized postseason implications. Two teams that currently hold winning records won’t make the cut.

title: How will Carson Beck do against Rams on Sunday?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams under Sean McVay are 9-2 against rookie quarterbacks and that could be bad news for Carson Beck and the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. full_text: The Los Angeles Rams under Sean McVay are 9-2 against rookie quarterbacks and that could be bad news for Carson Beck and the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday. It also could be an awesome opportunity for Beck to show up the Rams and fellow rookie Ty Simpson who will be on the sidelines. If Beck wins, then that’d be a great start to a NFL career. If Beck loses against Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald, then perhaps that was to be expected. We’ll have to tune in on Sunday to see Beck is another win for the Rams against rookie signal callers, or if he earns the tough win. How have rookie QBs fared historically vs. Sean McVay and the Rams? (ramswire) “Historically, rookie quarterbacks have struggled against the Rams. The odds are against Beck to buck that trend; Arizona is a 9.5-point underdog in this game, making the Rams heavy favorites despite being on the road Rookie QB stats vs. Rams since 2017 With McVay as the head coach, the Rams are 9-2 against rookie quarterbacks, according to Stathead . The only two rookies to beat the Rams were Caleb Williams in 2024 and Tua Tagovailoa in 2020. Tagovailoa only threw for 93 yards and one touchdown in that shocking win against Jared Goff and the Rams, while Williams had just 157 yards and a score in the Bears ‘ 24-18 win over Los Angeles in 2024.“ Week 10 picks: Experts predict Rams won’t get upset by Cardinals again (sports.yahoo) “The Los Angeles Rams head into Week 10 battered and bruised , but with a winning record for the first time all season. They’ll also take on an Arizona Cardinals team that upset them in Week 6. A win would help the Rams keep pace for the Wild Card as well as deliver the team’s first divisional win in 2026. It’ll be an interesting showdown given how well the Rams defense performed in Week 9 with Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett finally on the field together, especially given they’ll take on rookie quarterback Carson Beck and a similarly-injured Cardinals offense. Arizona is also without running back Jeremiyah Love and receiver Michael Wilson. The Rams, meanwhile, won’t have Puka Nacua, Davante Adams or Jordan Whittington in this game. NFL experts are not expecting an upset this time around. Los Angeles received all 52 picks across seven major outlets, with no analyst picking the Cardinals.“ Los Angeles Rams Announce Myles Garrett Decision Amid Significant Updates (heavy.com) ““Guys that will be DNPs: Myles Garrett. He’ll be questionable for the game. He’s feeling good. It’s more of just getting him feeling as good as possible. He’s had a really good week, played a bunch of snaps, and expect him to be able to build on that. But we’re being smart with him,” McVay told reporters on November 13. “Steve Avila will be listed as out with his hamstring. Trent McDuffie and Kam Curl will both be limited for practice today and listed as questionable. And then, Terrance Ferguson will be out for the game as well.” The most encouraging sign of Garrett’s status for Sunday is that he took the podium to speak with the media to close out the week.“ Rams’ Myles Garrett Among Multiple Questionable Players for Week 10 (sports.yahoo) “Garrett has been on the injury report with a knee ailment, which limited him on both Wednesday and Thursday. Per Rams reporter Stu Jackson , the defensive end is now questionable. In addition to Garrett, cornerback Trent McDuffie and safety Kam Curl are also questionable. McVay did state that he expects Garrett to play and “feels good” about Curl, which may likely lead to both suiting up for the Cardinals matchup. However, McDuffie is more of a worry, and his response over the weekend to working out will determine if he can play.“ Rams’ Myles Garrett expected to play at Arizona despite missing practice (mymotherlode) “Garrett was largely pleased with his performance, in which he played 61.5% of the defensive snaps, apart from needing to build up his endurance and address what he felt was a slow get-off time. “I’m sure Next Gen or PFF or somebody would tell me it wasn’t too bad,” Garrett said. “It felt terrible to me.” McDuffie is dealing with a back injury that forced him to miss the Rams’ third straight win last week, getting them over .500 for the first time this season at 5-4. McVay expressed optimism he would be able to play, provided McDuffie felt good coming out of Friday’s workout. “He was rolling, you know, doing a lot of good stuff yesterday,” McVay said. The ongoing issues with the Rams’ two marquee offseason acquisitions is indicative of their larger injury crisis that has threatened a campaign that began with them as Super Bowl betting favorites. Los Angeles is so beat up that star wide receiver Puka Nacua was placed on injured reserve Thursday to free up a roster spot, a reversal from what McVay had indicated earlier in the week when he cited the limited number of IR slots remaining to be able to bring players back later in the season. “Some things changed where we needed that spot because of all the moving pieces,” said McVay, while adding that nothing has changed with the timeline for Nacua’s return from knee and toe injuries.“ Rams’ $71 million injury nightmare among NFL’s worst (sports.yah00) “The Rams have watched a parade of Pro Bowlers, All-Pros and established starters limp into the training room this season, including Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Davante Adams and Puka Nacua. Garrett, the two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year , finally returned in Week 9 after undergoing knee surgery. Meanwhile, Watson is lost for the season , Adams remains sidelined with a hamstring injury, and Nacua is dealing with knee ligament sprains and turf toe. It’s enough to make the Rams’ medical staff consider asking for overtime pay. Believe it or not, the Rams aren’t even the most injured team in California, at least according to RotoWire’s formula.“ FAA flight debacle could disrupt Rams, Chargers, 49ers; NFL responds (nypost) “The Rams have spent all week preparing for the Cardinals. Now, an unprecedented travel nightmare could force them to prepare for a road trip of an entirely different kind. A nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday afternoon has thrown weekend travel plans into chaos, potentially affecting several NFL teams scheduled to fly to their respective games Saturday. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the shutdown about 1:15 p.m. PT, citing a communications issue affecting air traffic control centers across the country.“ Rams injury report: Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie questionable vs. Cardinals (ramswire) “Heading into Sunday’s game, the Rams will have three players listed as questionable: Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie and Kam Curl. Garrett isn’t practicing on Friday, as Sean McVay said the Rams are just “being smart” with him. McVay expects Garrett to play, saying that he’s “feeling good” and building on a strong performance last week. McDuffie and Curl will be limited in practice, and the Rams will see how they feel before determining their statuses for Sunday’s game. McDuffie has missed three of the last four games but McVay said earlier in the week that he’s “optimistic” about a return on Sunday. Curl didn’t practice at all last week due to a foot injury and still managed to play against the Commanders.“ A Duel in the Desert: Los Angeles Rams vs Arizona Cardinals Preview (lastwordonsports) ““One of the calling cards for our group, and is always an expectation, is we play with passion and energy, and I think we would all agree that (the first game against the Cardinals) wasn’t quite up to our standards,” McVay said . Los Angeles will likely rely on running 13 personnel while several of their best receivers are sidelined with injuries. Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford must spread the targets in order to keep Arizona’s defense off guard. “It’s not difficult to pull the trigger, I trust those guys,” Stafford said .“ Sean McVay reveals real reason why Rams suddenly changed minds on Puka…

full_text: Week 10 has the 5-4 Los Angeles Rams taking the short hop over the state line for a Sunday November 15 meeting with the 3-6 Arizona Cardinals. Kickoff from State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona is set for 1:05 p.m. PST. L.A. looks to avenge a humiliating Week 6 18-16 defeat to the Cards. In that tilt, Arizona used a balanced run/pass attack to control the game flow, to the tune of a 35-25 minute advantage in time of possession. Injuries have decimated the Rams wide receiver corps, Puka Nacua (WR#1) and Davante Adams (WR#2) are on the Injured Reserve List, as is backup (120 offensive reps) and kickoff returner Jordan Whittington. The Rams will fill this void with Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, rookie CJ Daniels, Xavier Smith, and Brennan Presley, who have a combined total of 18 catches on 36 targets for 261 yards and one score in 2026. With the state of the receiver room in flux, the Rams should look to run early and often in Arizona. Kyren Williams and Blake Corum have given L.A. a solid inside/outside rush attack. Williams, working primarily between the tackles, has shown an innate ability to make the first tackler miss and create yards after contact. Corum effectuates his yards off tackle, bursting through the slightest of openings and showing the acceleration to break runs outside and scoot in open field. The Rams offensive line is #1 in ESPN’s run block win rate . Right tackle Warren McClendon (#2) and center Coleman Shelton (#5) are amongst the NFL Top 5 in this category. Here’s how to follow the game! title: The Fernando Mendoza era marks a sizeable shift for rebuilding Raiders
summary: Nandomania is upon Raider Nation. By trading former starter Kirk Cousins for a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, the Las Vegas Raiders are turning to the top pick in the 2026 draft Fernando Mendoza at quarterback. The move from a 38-year-old veteran to the 23-year-old rookie marks a sizeable shift for the Silver […]
full_text: (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Nandomania is upon Raider Nation. By trading former starter Kirk Cousins for a third-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, the Las Vegas Raiders are turning to the top pick in the 2026 draft Fernando Mendoza at quarterback. The move from a 38-year-old veteran to the 23-year-old rookie marks a sizeable shift for the Silver & Black. “Our expectation is for him to lead the offense, to lead the operation, and to go play a game here Sunday and be the leader of the team, be the leader of the offense,” Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak said of Mendoza. “We have to prepare him and give him a lot of reps to get him comfortable. So, our expectation is for him to lead the offense.” Standing 6-foot-5 and 225 pounds, Mendoza brings NFL-size with a livelier arm and fresh legs with mobility to the quarterback position, as opposed to Cousins. But where the veteran has the rook beat is game experience. While Cousins may be a statue as a pocket passer, he did provide his younger counterpart an ideal mentor and sounding board. And Las Vegas is banking on the nine games Mendoza sat and watched Cousins operate provided a blueprint for the rookie to follow. And what an opponent for Mendoza to make his first start against: The Seattle Seahawks. “Like I said, this is a new experience. It’s great. It’s against a fantastic opponent. However, I have so much trust in the coaching staff, in the front office, and my teammates and the leaders of the team to go out there and best support everybody’s 1/11th, so we can do our job to the best ability.” While Seattle is quite shaky offensively — ranking 18th in points scored and 17th in yards gained under rookie offensive coordinator Brian Fleury — head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald has the Seahawks defense as one of the top units in the NFL. #Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza shared a statement thanking Kirk Cousins and his family: “It would’ve been really easy for Kirk to be a little more dismissive. He had me with open arms and has taught me so many things. … He shared it with no restrictions or constraints.” 🥹 pic.twitter.com/rUhol5ChiB — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) November 11, 2026 If both Mendoza and Kubiak are to get the Raiders aerial attack on track this Sunday, they’ll have to do it against the Seahawks’ top-ranked passing defense which is ranked No. 1 in air yards allowed (1,396). Seattle is also allowing the fourth-least passing touchdowns (nine) and have racked up the sixth-most interceptions (eight). Both the Raiders quarterback and head coach are eager to meet the challenge head-on, though. “It is, yeah. And every week in the NFL is tough, and this is the best defense in the NFL,” Kubiak said when asked about Mendoza’s start against a top-tier Seahawks defense being invaluable. “And again, he’s got to go do his job and not worry about a whole lot else. Everybody does their 1/11th, and everyone around him elevates their play.” Notice that 1/11th that both Mendoza and Kubiak were quick to drop during their respective times at the podium during media availability this week leading up the Week 10 matchup with the Seahawks? Kubiak’s offense epitomizes the all-11 approach. Ranked eighth in the NFL in points scored (238) and 15th in yards gained (2,979), Las Vegas passing game is ranked fifth in air yards (2,337) and are third-best in touchdowns (20). The offensive line — which has showcased much better pass protection ability than run blocking — kept Cousins upright for those 20 touchdowns and the expectation is the group doing the same for Mendoza. The stronger arm talent the Indiana product brings to the table should pay dividends for Raiders pass catchers like tight end Brock Bowers (team-leading 48 receptions, 658 yards, and six touchdowns), fleet-footed wide receiver Tre Tucker (33 receptions for 529 yards and four touchdowns), and running back Ashton Jeanty (42 receptions for 371 yards and three touchdowns. Add tight end Michael Mayer (39 catches for 388 yards and a touchdown), and Mendoza has weaponary at his disposal. Seattle HC Mike Macdonald on Raiders Klint Kubiak from NFL Owner's Meeting #raiders #raidernation #LasVegasRaiders #nfl #lasvegasraidersonsi pic.twitter.com/8PBukAXDVe — Hondo Carpenter (@HondoCarpenter) March 30, 2026 Las Vegas’ ground game is in the pits, however, and is ranked dead-last in yards gained (642) and yards per carry average (2.9). Much of this is due to lack of trench dominance and opposing defenses loading the box with eight defenders knowing Cousins presents zero threat to scramble and take off with his legs. Perhaps the Mendoza dynamic changes that for Kubiak’s offense? “But, hey, go through your progression, and obviously if it’s not there, you’ve got to go run the football. And then when you’re running the football, how do you protect yourself so that you can get us to the next down, because we need you available for the whole season,” Kubiak said regarding Mendoza trusting his eyes, staying in the pocket, and run as a last resort rather than too quickly. “You’re not trying to sell out for a yard on first-and-10, so it’s an ongoing learning process. But that’s also why when you’re selecting men in the draft, you identify their instincts. I liked Fernando’s instincts in college, and it’s his first NFL game. So, we’re all going to see. But I’m excited for his opportunity and just for the whole offense to go play together.” We’re going to find out if Kubiak’s quarterback-whisperer ways can transfer to Mendoza as it has with Sam Darnold (during the Raiders head coach’s time as Seattle offensive coordinator last season) and Cousins. While this game features the debut of Mendoza and matching up against Macdonald’s defense, underneath all this is this simple item between the Raiders and Seahawks: Kubiak misses Macdonald’s defense (Las Vegas’ group is led by rookie defensive coordinator Rob Leonard and ranks dead last in points allowed (268) and yards yielded (3,469)) and Macdonald misses Kubiak’s offense. Quote of Note “Kirk has taught me a multitude of lessons, but two of the ones that stick out right now from your question is, number one, always being prepared and doing everything possible you can to prepare yourself to best serve your teammates, to best serve the organization. So you go out there Sunday, regardless of the result, no doubt in your mind that you did everything possible to give your team and teammates the best chance to perform and win. And second is to be yourself. He’s always told everybody on the team, and he was a great leader and captain on the team and really brought us together and had a lot of togetherness. So that’s something that I look to exemplify and take from his lessons.” —Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza on what lessons from former starter Kirk Cousins sticks out
author: Ray Aspuria

title: How does Seattle Seahawks’ offense look with Drew Lock at quarterback for Week 10 matchup against Las Vegas Raiders?
summary: Week 10 features an old-school AFC West rivalry as the then-Oakland, now Las Vegas Raiders and Seattle Seahawks had plenty of noteworthy divisional battles in the ‘80s and ‘90s before the NFL’s realignment that pushed Seattle into the NFC. To preview this weekend’s matchup, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Field […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 10 features an old-school AFC West rivalry as the then-Oakland, now Las Vegas Raiders and Seattle Seahawks had plenty of noteworthy divisional battles in the ‘80s and ‘90s before the NFL’s realignment that pushed Seattle into the NFC. To preview this weekend’s matchup , Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Field Gulls, and John Gilbert was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Seahawks for Raider Nation. Q: Sam Darnold has already been ruled out, meaning Drew Lock will make his fourth appearance and third start this season. What’s the difference in the Seahawks’ offense with Lock at quarterback, and what’s the fanbase’s confidence level in him as the starter? A: In years past, the answer to this would hark back to Pete Carroll’s 2023 comments about Lock making a couple of boneheaded throws. But when Lock has played this season, he has done a phenomenal job protecting the football. Darnold has missed two full games and only played five snaps in the season opener against the New England Patriots. Yet in spite of that, he is tied with Matthew Stafford for the most interceptions thrown in the NFC. On the flip side, Lock has five touchdowns and no interceptions while starting twice and playing most of the game against the Patriots. Of course, both of Lock’s starts came against the Arizona Cardinals, and the Arizona defense has done a solid job helping opposing quarterbacks bolster their stat lines this season, so we’ll see what Lock can do against the Raiders. Q: Jaxon Smith-Njigba is coming off a season where he led the NFL with nearly 1,800 receiving yards and won Offensive Player of the Year. So far in 2026, he’s the first and currently only player to eclipse the 1,000-yard mark while averaging about 10 yards per game more than he did last year . What makes JSN such a tough cover? Any suggestions for how to keep him in check? A: JSN has simply become a monster. He’s a very smooth and fluid route runner, and at the foundation of his greatness is the simple fact that all of his route stems look the same, making it impossible for defensive backs to anticipate what is coming. Add in great hands, a phenomenal work ethic and the reality that he is far and away the most dangerous offensive weapon in the Seattle arsenal. It’s a recipe to continue to feed him the ball until defenses can find a way to slow him down. Teams have tried almost everything to slow JSN down, but a consistent weakness has not yet been found. Jamming him at the line doesn’t stop him. Bracketing doesn’t stop him. Whatever opponents do, he just continues to find ways to get open and keep the offense moving. Q: Seattle’s rushing attack ranks 18th in yards per game, 25th in yards per carry and 27th in EPA per rush, according to Sumer Sports . Are the issues as simple as the offense missing Klint Kubiak and Kenneth Walker III? Has adding Quenton Nelson helped at all? A: Losing Kenneth Walker III to the Chiefs in free agency certainly hurt. The two biggest things the Seattle run game has missed for most of the first half of the season were the explosiveness and the ball security that Walker brought to the table. Yes, he had a style that could be infuriating at times, as he had a tendency to try to bounce so many runs outside looking for the big play. But the simple fact is that he has the burst and speed to create an outsized number of explosive plays, even while consistently finishing in the bottom half of the league in success rate. During his four seasons in Seattle, Walker fumbled a total of three times on 821 regular-season rushing attempts, while his replacements (Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson and George Holani) have put the ball on the ground six times in 195 rushing attempts so far this season. With that said, Zach Charbonnet is back in the lineup after tearing his ACL in the 2025 postseason, and his presence has been an instant upgrade at the position. Charbonnet is never going to present the big-play threat that Walker brought to the field on every rushing attempt, but Charbonnet is a disciplined back who will follow his blocking, while providing solid pass protection from the backfield in passing situations. As for Quenton Nelson, so far the trade has produced more excitement and hype than on-field production. Nelson apparently suffered a minor knee injury before the trade and had a procedure to address the issue. As such, with the Seahawks enjoying a bye week after facing off against the Raiders, he likely won’t be back in action again until Week 12 against the San Francisco 49ers. Q: Imagine you’re Kubiak game-planning for Fernando Mendoza’s first start against the vaunted Seahawks’ defense. How would you attack the defense and give the rookie quarterback his best chance at having success? Keep in mind that the Raiders are one of the few teams that are worse at running the ball than the Seahawks are. A: Where Kubiak really seemed to excel in Seattle was creating tendencies, or the appearance of tendencies, and then in high-leverage situations making it look like the offense is following that tendency, only to break off for a big play. So, whatever tendencies the Raiders offense has put on tape through the first half of the season, I expect those tendencies to be thrown out the window at key times within the games as Kubiak looks for big plays. The reality is that while the Seahawks defense is great, so far in 2026 the Seahawks offense hasn’t shown to be on par with the 2025 group, and between conservative playcalling and Drew Lock battling oblique and elbow issues, it might only take a couple of big plays for the Raiders to play spoilers against the defending champs. Q: Between Leonard Williams, Byron Murphy II, Devon Witherspoon, Ernest Jones IV and Nick Emmanwori, Seattle’s defense is filled with studs. If you had to pick one to deem the biggest key or X-factor for the unit, who would it be and why? A: As cliché as it sounds, there is no one piece that makes the defense tick. What makes Mike Macdonald’s defenses so good is that all eleven players are on the same page, doing their jobs at a high level. All of the big names on defense play key roles, but as a whole the group has enough depth that a single missing piece doesn’t send things off the rails. With that all said, everything starts in the trenches. So if Williams and Murphy aren’t able to do their thing up front, it leaves the rest of the defense hanging.
author: Matt Holder

title: Raiders Mailbag: Could John Spytek have gotten bigger return from Minnesota Vikings in Kirk Cousins trade?
summary: After trading starting quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a third-round pick ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 10 game against the Seattle Seahawks will forever be known as Fernando Mendoza’s first regular-season start for the Raiders. Of course, that’s the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images After trading starting quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a third-round pick ahead of Tuesday’s deadline, the Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 10 game against the Seattle Seahawks will forever be known as Fernando Mendoza’s first regular-season start for the Raiders . Of course, that’s the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! A: I get that a lot of people feel like the Raiders didn’t get a big enough return for Cousins, and initially, I was surprised they didn’t get more, too. I felt like John Spytek could have at least gotten an escalator on the pick where, if the Vikings made the NFC Championship, Super Bowl or whatever with Cousins, the pick becomes a second-rounder. However, all of the reporting after the fact has been that Minnesota wasn’t willing to go higher than a third for Cousins. So, if he wasn’t going to be the starter in Las Vegas for much longer, at least Spytek managed to get a Top 100 pick from a player who wasn’t going to be on next year’s roster and probably wasn’t going to be contributing for much longer this year anyway. Why wouldn’t the Vikings budge? Well, this is the same organization that moved on from Cousins a few years ago because they felt like they’d never be able to make a deep playoff run with him. Now that he’s older and didn’t join the team until halfway through the season, I’d imagine the logic is similar. Essentially, Minnesota was willing to take a chance that the 38-year-old can salvage the campaign, but not at the cost of potentially jeopardizing the club’s future, and drew a line at the third-rounder. Q: Can you please help me understand just what this team is doing? Trading your starting QB sends a signal that you’re no longer competing; you’re rebuilding. If that is the case, why do you keep your best trade asset in Maxx Crosby, who could bring you higher-round draft picks? Many people feel like the Raiders won’t win another game and fear for Mendoza. A: To be honest, I don’t think my answer is going to be satisfactory for you. It’s never been a secret that this is a rebuild year for the Raiders. They put a heavy emphasis on getting younger in the offseason, and it was always clear that Kirk Cousins was a bridge-gap starter until Mendoza was ready to start. The Cousins trade doesn’t happen if John Spytek and Klint Kubiak don’t think the latter is true. Spytek even said that the organization feels it can still win in the second half of this season with the rookie behind center. As far as not trading Crosby, I can agree that it’d make sense to try and get picks for him. However, the coaching staff and front office seem to think what he brings as a leader is more valuable to the culture that Kubiak is trying to build than a couple of draft picks. Also, keeping Crosby ties back to Spytek and Kubiak thinking they can stay in the playoff hunt with Mendoza. Now, if that plan falls flat and the team struggles down the stretch, maybe the strategy changes in the offseason and they look to move Crosby for picks again. But right now, the team’s brass appears comfortable seeing how the rest of the campaign plays out with the No. 1 pick leading the charge. A: I think you’re on the right track here where Kubiak’s game plan is going to be to get the ball out of Mendoza’s hands quickly and give him some easy throws, especially early on. There might not be a worse defense to face for a quarterback’s first NFL start given how many certified dudes the Seahawks have and how confusing Mike Macdonald’s scheme is. So, I think we’ll see a good amount of predetermined throws via screens, RPOs and bootlegs to simplify the rookie’s reads and try to neutralize Seattle’s pass rush. And of course, if there’s ever a game for the rushing attack to finally hit its stride, it’s this one. A: If I’m Macdonald, I’m throwing the book at Mendoza by giving him a lot of pressure looks pre-snap and changing the picture post-snap. Basically, the strategy is to try to overwhelm and confuse the rookie as much as possible so that he starts thinking too much and either holds onto the ball too long or makes a mistake that leads to a turnover. That’s why I think Kubiak should start the game with the predetermined quick throws mentioned above. Take the thinking off Fernando’s plate initially and let him get into a rhythm to build some confidence before opening up the playbook later on. To use a cross-sport reference, it’d be like a jump shooter looking to get fouled early so he can get to the line and see a few balls go through the hoop before letting it rip from three. A: I just want to start by giving you a hard time about asking a “two-part question” when there are four questions in here, LOL! I think Brock Bowers was always expected to be the primary receiver, and the actual receivers were viewed as complementary pieces. Bowers is doing a pretty good job of filling that role, seeing as he’s putting up wide receiver numbers, ranking tied for 14th in receptions (48), 10th in yards (658) and tied for sixth in touchdowns (six) among all pass-catchers, not just tight ends. And that’s after missing two games. As long as he’s around, the ‘WR1’ issue is overblown, in my opinion. On top of that, I think Tre Tucker has been a solid No. 2 this season. He ranks in the top 25 of receivers in catches (33, tied for 25th), yards (529, 17th) and touchdowns (four, tied for 11th). It also wouldn’t be surprising to me if Tucker is even more productive with Mendoza, given the latter brings more arm strength to the table than Cousins did. Now, Tucker is an impending free agent, and it might make more sense to save money for Bowers’ extension. So, wide receiver might still be an offseason need this year, but it doesn’t need to be a top priority if the plan is to open up the checkbook for the “football robot from heaven”. With Bech, he’s never been a great separator and has always been more reliant on winning contested catches. That was the book on him coming out of TCU, and it has shown up during his limited playing time in the NFL so far. He was/is a decent route runner; he just isn’t a high-level athlete to explode out of cuts and generate a lot of separation. He can win by being physical at the top of the route, but that isn’t going to result in wide-open targets. However, Bech has only run 59 routes this season, per Pro Football Focus , and just 19 in the two games since he returned from injury. So it’s too small of a sample size for me to say definitively that’s been the issue this year. A: I’d like to see Jackson Powers-Johnson get a shot at left guard, but I don’t think it will happen. One of the frustrations I have with Kubiak is that he seems to be too loyal to Spencer Buford. The Athletic’s Sam Warren didn’t say that directly when he joined Marcus and me on Tape Don’t Lie a couple of weeks ago , but Warren did mention that the coaching staff thinks higher of Burford than what his perception is outside of the building. Also, I’m sure some people are tired of me saying this; I get the feeling JPJ won’t be on the roster after this season. Unless an injury happens where he gets put back into the lineup and plays well, I think it’ll be a similar situation to Tyree Wilson, where Powers-Johnson gets shopped and traded in the offseason. A: Let’s slow down here for a second. Marcus and I aren’t saying Mike Washington Jr. is a bust. Last week just highlighted that he isn’t ready to take over as the lead running back ahead of Ashton Jeanty, which has always been the expectation for the fourth-round pick. summary: The Miami Dolphins have won just one game over the first nine weeks of the 2026 NFL season. This year, for the Dolphins, however, the fans seem to be accepting that this is only […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Ollie Gordon II #0 of the Miami Dolphins in action against the Detroit Lions at Hard Rock Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins have won just one game over the first nine weeks of the 2026 NFL season. Having already passed their bye week, the Dolphins are 1-7, which would typically lead to a frustrated fanbase itching for change. This year, for the Dolphins, however, the fans seem to be accepting that this is only the first season of a long-term rebuild, understanding that losses now may lead to victories in the future. Things are not all well in Miami, though. This week, two major pieces of the starting lineup landed on injured reserve. Quarterback Malik Willis heads to the sideline for at least four weeks with a groin injury; season-ending surgery hasn’t been ruled out, but there is hope he can return in a few weeks. The news was not as good for defensive tackle Zach Sieler, who tore his biceps muscle last week. The injury occurred on the first snap of Miami’s game against the Detroit Lions, but the veteran played through it for the rest of the game. Now he will undergo surgery and will need around six months of recovery time before he is cleared to return to football activities. Miami faces the Indianapolis Colts tomorrow as the NFL’s Week 10 schedule continues. Despite Indianapolis struggling this year, earning just two wins against seven losses in the first half of the season, the oddsmakers see the Colts still likely to win this game. The latest FanDuel Sportsbook odds have the Colts favored by 3.5 points over Miami. Dolphins fan confidence The highlight of the season for the Dolphins came in Week 7, when they beat the New York Jets. Our Week 8 SB Nation Reacts fan confidence survey reflected the victory with a 97 percent positive rating for the Dolphins. It was the high-water mark of the year, and the only week in which our survey topped the 90 percent mark. At least until this week. Going toe-to-toe with the Detroit Lions for much of Week 9 encouraged the fans that brighter days are coming. The survey opened before the news of the injuries to Willis and Sieler broke, but then ran throughout the rest of the week, and it remained up above 90 percent all week. When the poll closed, 91 percent of the responses indicated the Dolphins are headed in the right direction. How will tomorrow’s game against the Colts affect next week’s survey? We will be back early next week to ask for your updated confidence in Miami’s direction. title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 9
summary: When you lose 19-9 in a game where your offense only crosses midfield a handful of times, it’s usually best to burn the tape and move on. That may be especially true for the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins’ future. […]
full_text: When you lose 19-9 in a game where your offense only crosses midfield a handful of times, it’s usually best to burn the tape and move on. That may be especially true for the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins’ future. While the offense struggled as a whole, player development doesn’t stop because of one ugly afternoon, and that’s especially true for two young guards expected to be part of the foundation moving forward. Each week, we take a closer look at Proctor and Savaiinaea and examine what analysts are saying about their most recent performances. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 51.2 48.6 64.9 10/11, vs. Bengals 66 (100%) 0 72.7 74.9 52.2 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 59.6 58.2 61.3 DNP 11/8, vs. Lions 57 (100%) 0 57.3 50.2 72.6 Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 49.5 44.6 77.5 10/11, vs. Bengals 18 (27%) 0 45.4 44.7 78.4 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 49.4 53.5 31.4 11/1, vs. Patriots 65 (100%) 1 49.7 51.9 63.4 11/8, vs. Lions 57 (100%) 0 45.8 46.0 44.3 What We Learned Listen, it was not a good week for the offensive line – if you were hoping for a bounce-back effort after a rough outing against the Patriots, the tape from the Detroit Lions game offered very little comfort. While much of the post-game attention has been directed toward Aaron Brewer and Austin Jackson, the entire unit struggled against a physical Detroit front. Alain Poupart over at Sports Illustrated called the offensive line the team’s most disappointing position group based on PFF rankings (I know, I know): Brewer is ranked 17th out of 36 qualifying centers. Paul is ranked 47th out of 71 tackles. Jackson is ranked 71st out of 71 tackles. That’s not great, Bob. Proctor is ranked 35th among 75 guards. Jonah Savaiinaea is 69th among 75 guards. For Kadyn Proctor, while it was undeniably a rough afternoon against the Lions, there is still plenty of reason for long-term optimism. His individual tape showed some correctable rookie mistakes, such as getting too flat on a second-quarter power play and completely missing his linebacker assignment. However, he also flashed his high-end potential later in the game by quickly recognizing a slanting defensive tackle on a trap concept and stopping on a dime to seal the block. While there were instances of missing second-level blocks, Proctor still played with physicality and had some highlight blocks. He continues to flash the talent that made him a first-round pick, and his mistakes largely look like growing pains. The conversation around Jonah Savaiinaea, however, is becoming a bit more concerning. The Lions frequently isolated him in space by putting five men on the line of scrimmage, and Jonah struggled mightily, particularly when giving up inside moves. On one notable power play, indecision caused Jonah to completely pass up his assigned defender, blowing up the timing of the run. After a solid first three weeks of the season, his recent tape has looked a lot like his 2025 rookie struggles, when he ranked last among all guards. While it is still too early to make a definitive call on his career trajectory, it’s fair to ask if he may settle in as a below-average starter rather than the long-term answer we hoped for. Maybe we’ll see more of that early-season tape against the Colts. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .

This week, we’re going to be seeing the return of the Kirk, as Kirk Cousins will take over at quarterback for the Vikings at the place where he played his last game as quarterback for the Vikings: Lambeau Field in Green Bay. It was there in 2023 that he tore his Achilles tendon in a Vikings win over the Packers, kicking off the spiral at the quarterback position the Vikings have been on since then. Will the change mean big things for the Minnesota offense? I would like to think so. . .I would like to hope so. With that, let’s get to the bets. Kirk Cousins passing yardage : Over 232.5 yards (-114) Coming into this week, Cousins is averaging 260 passing yards/game, and he hasn’t exactly been throwing to Three Deep out in Las Vegas or anything. The hope is that Cousins is going to be able to do what Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz have failed to do all season: Find the open receiver and hit them. The reports we’ve seen coming from practices this week are that it’s like Cousins never left, so he still knows the offense. If the Vikings can keep the Packers’ pass rush off of him, he should be able to make some plays on Sunday. Justin Jefferson receiving yardage : Over 80.5 yards (-114) Usually, I put this bet out there just because Justin Jefferson is. . .well, Justin Jefferson. This week, however, there are a few other reasons to lean this way. Namely because T.J. Hockenson is out, Jauan Jennings is out, and Jordan Addison is questionable to play with a thumb injury. To put it simply, the number of other options that may be available in the receiving corps could potentially be limited. Having said that, there is nobody happier to see Kirk Cousins at quarterback than Justin Jefferson, as when Jefferson was setting records all over the place early in his career, it was #8 throwing him the ball. The magic comes back, starting on Sunday. Parlay : Vikings +3 and Under 42.5 points (+218) Again, as I think I’ve said in previous weeks when I’ve put this sort of bet out there, the only Vikings game this season that hit the “over” came back in Week 1 between these two teams. I’m not going to suggest that you bet the over on a Vikings game. . .not with this defense. That said, I think this game gets the Vikings back on the winning track, as the offense will (hopefully) be able to sustain some drives and not have their defense on the field for forty minutes so that they can get the job done in the fourth quarter as well. Those are the bets I’m looking at for this week, ladies and gentlemen. Are there any that you’ve got your eye on in this one?

Some other McKay one liners … On the Struggling Buccaneers On winless streaks and performance: After an 0–26 start, he joked, “Three or four plane crashes and we’re in the playoffs”, and lamented, “We didn’t tackle well today, but we made up for it by not blocking”. He also noted they could “Can’t stop the pass or the run, otherwise we’re in great shape” and requested a neutral site because they couldn’t play at home or on the road. On Coaching & Football Philosophy On strategy and players: He famously dismissed football emotion by comparing it to his wife Corky and defended giving O.J. Simpson the ball constantly because “it isn’t very heavy”. Down 17–0 at halftime to Notre Dame, he offered the simple math that “If you don’t score more than 17 points, you’ll lose” (USC rallied to win). On Recruiting & Fan Pressure On family and fans: When recruiting his son J.K. McKay to USC, he noted he had the advantage that he “slept with his mother”, and threatened to pay his way to “Peking” if he chose Stanford over USC. To handle hostile fan bases, he joked that he bought up all the rope in Los Angeles to prevent being hung in effigy. Bum Phillips had some funny quotes too … On Coaching & Football On Job Security & Rivals: Quips included noting that coaches are split into “them that’s fired and them that’s gonna be fired”, and praising Don Shula’s ability to “take his’n and beat your’n and take your’n and beat his’n”. On Team Struggles & Drive: Famously remarked, “The harder we played, the behinder we got”, criticized uncoachable extremes, and vowed that after knocking on the Super Bowl door, “Next year we’re going to kick the son of a bitch in!”. On Life & Himself Self-Deprecation & Humor: Remarked he didn’t mind people thinking he was stupid, just didn’t want to prove it, didn’t mind being called Bum without a “you” in front of it, and joked that he brought his wife on road trips because “she’s too ugly to kiss goodbye”. The Astrodome: Noted that “Mama always said that if it can’t rain on you, you’re indoors” when explaining why he didn’t wear his cowboy hat inside the stadium. … sorry, I digressed. I have seen the “report” that the new Vikings regime is down on Caleb Banks and Norse4life posted a link to the story in a feed. Thanks. I will say that it is interesting and curious at best. Banks missed almost all of his final season at Florida and then broke his foot at the 2026 NFL Combine, which kept him out of OTAs, minicamp, and most of training camp. Judging a 6’6″, 327-pound rookie who missed an entire offseason of conditioning on just about 100 NFL snaps is an overreaction. Also, and more importantly, you have to believe the BFlo had significant input into the Banks and Golday picks. If someone is going to criticize the Banks pick because he is not doing much yet then they should “man up” and criticize BFlo too. Problem with that is the Vikings have one of the top defensea in the NFL. I believe the team knows exactly what it is doing with both Banks and Golday and are grooming them for their opportunity just like they did with Dallas Turner. One good thing about Cousins this year is … 2026 Situational Splits by Game Score Breaking down Cousins’s 2026 passing numbers across CBS Sports and NFL.com situational logs reveals a sharp contrast in volume and efficiency depending on the scoreboard: Game State : Cmp / Att : Comp % : Yards : Yds / Att : TD : INT : Sacks : Passer Rating Ahead (Leading) : 28 / 52 : 53.8% : 221 : 4.2 : 4 : 2 : 2 : 74.3 Tied : 44 / 68 : 64.7% : 511 : 7.5 : 4 : 1 : 4 : 100.8 Behind (Trailing) : 130 / 195 : 66.7% : 1,608 : 8.2 : 12 : 5 : 5 : 101.8 Total : 202 / 315 : 64.1% : 2,340 : 7.4 : 20 : 8 : 11 : 97.1 While nearly 69% of Cousins’s passing yards (1,608 of 2,340) came while trailing, looking closely at game scripts shows that most of those yards came in competitive, one-score losses rather than true garbage time. title: Sunday Patriots Notes: 10 things we learned in Munich
summary: The New England Patriots are in the German city of Munich this week, and set to take on the Detroit Lions for the sixth international game in franchise history. The team of head coach Mike Vrabel made the trip on Thursday, and so did a select group of media representatives — including from Pats Pulpit. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are in the German city of Munich this week, and set to take on the Detroit Lions for the sixth international game in franchise history. The team of head coach Mike Vrabel made the trip on Thursday, and so did a select group of media representatives — including from Pats Pulpit. Today’s edition of our Sunday Patriots Notes will therefore look a bit different, and not just serve as a wrap-up of the week that was but rather a look at the trip and its host city. 10 things we learned about the Patriots, Munich and the NFL 1. The Patriots have a balance to strike: All work and no play makes the Patriot a dull boy — it’s not quite as dramatic but flying to a different country to play a regular season game is obviously a difference experience for the players involved. For some of them, it is the first trip abroad in their lives meaning that they had to get passports and experience the challenges of transatlantic travel (more on that in a second). At the end of the day, it is still a work trip for the team and one that is being taken seriously. The Patriots, who are coming off a 45-27 loss against the Packers, have made that very clear: they want to bounce back from last week’s defeat and head into their bye week as the owners of a 6-4 record. (On a site note: the Lions do not get the benefit of a bye after the Germany trip; they already had theirs in Week 6). That said, they also did not spend the entire four-day journey in the team hotel either. For starters, players had practice and media obligations, and they were given some free time in the afternoons. Some of that was used on getting food — McDonalds received rave reviews from players such as center Jared Wilson because it offers chicken wings in Germany — while some participated in a guided tour of the city. One word to describe Munich? “Wow”‼️🤯 pic.twitter.com/ZiPp4arWPf — New England Patriots (@Patriots) November 14, 2026 2. Travel is a challenge: Brenden Schooler is not a stranger to flying to Europe. This week’s trip is the third in his five-year career after he already played in Frankfurt in 2023 and in London in 2024, two games the Patriots ended up losing. And yet even for a veteran such as himself travel is a challenge. The Patriots left from Providence on Thursday evening with the goal of getting some sleep in on the flight. The body still has to adjust to the six-hour time difference, and for Schooler that showed the following night: he woke up at 2:30 a.m. and before getting back to sleep hit the workout room in the team hotel to get a brief session in. Other players shared similar experiences. Getting those disruptions out of their way sooner rather than later was the plan behind an earlier-than-usual trip. The Patriots held a walkthrough practice in Munich on Thursday followed by a regular session and another walkthrough on Friday and Saturday, respectively. The Lions, meanwhile, took a different approach: they traveled 24 hours later, meaning their adjustment schedule is theoretically behind the Patriots’. And yet, head coach Dan Campbell is “very confident” in his decision. “We have got up and moved around, and I know that every eight hours here, we’re going to begin to acclimate,” he said , via Pride of Detroit’s Jeremy Reisman. “I know by the time we hit Sunday morning into that Sunday afternoon game, we’re going to be ready to go. So, we will be primed and ready, and I feel very good about our plan.” 3. Players have learned their lessons from prior international trips: Like Brenden Schooler, DeMario Douglas has also been part of the Patriots’ previous two journeys to Europe. And for him, one of the main goals this week was simply to “eat well” — something he apparently did not do in both Frankfurt and London. One of the reasons for that, however, might have been his own culinary choices: he went to a Five Guys the last time the Patriots played an international game. Lessons learned, one would assume. 4. Lorenz Metz is in the spotlight: Unless they are some big-name players on the back-nine of their careers, practice squadders enjoy a relatively anonymous life. Chances are that, until this week, you haven’t heard Lorenz Metz’s name mentioned often if at all whether you live in Germany or the United States. That all changed this week. Metz, who grew up an hour east of Munich, was made one of the faces of the operation. On Thursday, he took the podium alongside the likes of Drake Maye and Christian Gonzalez and drew considerable interest especially from the local media in the audience (in an unexpected twist, he also opted to answer all questions be they in English or German in his native language). Metz, who also organized and paid the traditional O-line dinner on Thursday night, will step out of the spotlight soon; carrying an international exception, he is ineligible to play on Sunday. For a few days, however, he was — at least in the eyes of the German media present — one of the headline names. 5. Getting to know Germany was on the to-do list: Yes, the Patriots made it very clear this was a work trip. However, they also mixed together work and fun in order to get familiar with their home country — both in their free time and in the meeting room: as Mike Vrabel noted, the team did a quiz asking players to name Germany’s neighboring countries. We didn’t get full results, but safety Craig Woodson said that his teammate Lorenz Metz managed to name “a couple” of the nine countries in question. 6. At least temporarily, Munich is all-NFL: Walking around the old town in Munich this week, you are confronted with a fascinating dichotomy. On the one hand, you see workers setting up Christmas markets and getting the city ready for the coming weeks. On the other hand, you see the NFL represented on every corner. Storefronts, flags, thousands in NFL gear — pro football has managed to take over a city typically dominated by soccer. The city itself also is actively trying to promote itself along the way, unsurprisingly. As part of the efforts, media members from both New England and Detroit were given a tour of the city including a dinner that can best be described as plentiful. Unsolicited tip: go to the new city hall and take the elevator up the tower for some of the best views of the city and, when the weather is right, the Alps. 7. Paranoia is a constant: It’s no secret that NFL teams are paranoid; they operate behind closed doors and making sure not to spill any of the tricks of their particular trade. That paranoia, it turns out, travels. Practicing at the FC Bayern Munich training facility in a southern suburb, the Patriots did not leave anything up to chance — to a point where they installed temporary walls to shield some of the view of the practice fields. 8. A pro-Lions crowd? When arriving in Munich on Thursday, you could the impression you made the trip to Detroit: from the people on the street to the atmosphere in the different team pubs, this was a definitive pro-Lions crowd. Part of it has to do with the contest being designated a Lions home game, and the city therefore hosting more events catered toward that particular fan base (there was, for example, a big Lions fan fest). It also is the first Lions international game since 2015, and first ever in Germany. However, the balance of crowd power has since shifted. The main reason for that simply seems to be the composition of the fan bases themselves, with the Patriots having more fans in Europe who don’t need to turn the trip into a four-day weekend. The Patriots also had another ace up their sleeves: the Tartan Army, Scottish soccer fans who were invited to visit the game by team owner Robert Kraft after they spent parts of the summer in Boston to support their country at the world cup. Now, they are in Munich supporting the Patriots. After the Scottish soccer fans took over Boston during the World Cup, Robert Kraft invited the Tartan Army to Germany to watch the Patriots play 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 #NFLonDAZN…

title: 3 things the Patriots have to do to beat the Lions
summary: The New England Patriots are taking Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions quite seriously. Not only do they want to wash the taste of last week’s 45-27 defeat versus Green Bay from their collective mouths, they also hope to enter the upcoming bye week with a 6-4 record and some much-needed momentum on their side. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots are taking Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions quite seriously. Not only do they want to wash the taste of last week’s 45-27 defeat versus Green Bay from their collective mouths, they also hope to enter the upcoming bye week with a 6-4 record and some much-needed momentum on their side. Doing so will not be easy; the Lions are a formidable opponent making the trip to Germany off a four-game winning streak. However, there are ways for the Patriots to defeat them and it starts with the following crucial areas. Stop Jahmyr Gibbs Jahmyr Gibbs is a problem. Just ask any team that has had to face him this season. Appearing in all eight of the Detroit Lions’ games, the versatile running back has gained more than 100 scrimmage yards six times. On the year, he is ranked first in the NFL with 1,132 of them and also has found the end zone a league-leading 11 times. He is the motor that powers an offense that has been among the most productive in football thus far in 2026. And, unsurprisingly, he is a player the New England Patriots are making sure to keep a close eye on this Sunday. “Gibbs is probably the best running back in the league right now as far as his target share, the amount of yards, in terms of how much offense he is producing by himself,” said safety Kevin Byard. “He’s the No. 1 target that we have to stop, for sure.” Joining the Lions as a first-round draft pick in 2023, Gibbs’ career is off to a red-hot start. He is ranked first in the NFL in touchdowns since starting his career (60) and second in scrimmage yards (6,161). He also was voted to the Pro Bowl in every season thus far. “Probably one of the best players in the NFL,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr at the FC Bayern Munich practice facility earlier this week. “He’s got the most touches, all-purpose yards, forced missed tackles, explosive runs. He’s a threat out of the backfield.” While the Lions offense as a whole is filled to the brim with talent — including quarterback Jared Goff, who isn’t going to be underestimated by the Patriots — Gibbs is the main man. The 24-year-old has touched the ball on over 40% of Detroit’s plays and is responsible for 37% of the team’s yardage output, despite only averaging 5.4 yards per touch. He also has scored 11 of 25 Detroit touchdowns this season. So, how do the Patriots actually stop him? Maybe by taking a page out of the Dolphins’ playbook. Miami didn’t do anything fancy with blitzes or stunts — they just built a wall, filled lanes quickly, and mostly swarmed well to keep Gibbs from getting more yards even when he broke tackles. He finished that game with a season-low 74 yards and a touchdown. Slow down the pass game They may not be the Packers, who had averaged 4.7 explosive pass plays per game entering their contest against the Patriots last week (before adding seven more to their tally), but the Lions are more than capable of putting pressure on New England’s pass defense as well. Another performance like last Sunday’s would therefore be a problem for the team. So, what do you do if you’re the Patriots? There are multiple ways to tackle this problem beyond just better execution from the players on the field, and they all start at the very most important spot: quarterback. Jared Goff may not be one of the NFL’s top-tier quarterbacks, but he has been pretty darn good getting the football to his weapons. That group is highlighted by the aforementioned Jahmyr Gibbs – just look at the numbers – but also includes other talented players in wide receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams as well as tight end Sam LaPorta. All of them are dangerous with the ball in their hands, so preventing it from getting there looks like a natural first step to success. In order to accomplish that particular goal against a player dubbed an “elite pocket passer” by the team this week, one position group in particular will be in the spotlight: the interior defensive line, and most prominently the top trio of Milton Williams, Christian Barmore and Cory Durden. They know it, too. “He’s one of the best in the league. If they keep him clean, he has a clean pocket, he can make any throw,” Williams explained. “They have a lot of weapons over there. Good offensive line. If he can play with a clean pocket and time to throw, he can make any throw with any quarterback in this league.” Whether or not the Patriots can bring pressure remains to be seen, but the Lions have been good at keeping Jared Goff clean so far this season. He has been pressured on only 31.8% of his dropbacks, according to Pro Football Focus, the seventh-lowest number in the league. It might be time for the Patriots’ interior duo of Williams and Barmore to live up to their quite sizable paychecks. Block Detroit’s pass rush There is one universal truth when it comes to passing the football: it’s hard to do so when your quarterback is on his butt. Drake Maye, to his credit, hasn’t had to experience this quite as much as he had to earlier in his career. That said, while he is still pressured at the fourth-highest rate in the NFL this season (43.3%) and ranked eighth in most sacks taken (20). Those numbers seeing an increase on Sunday could very well happen. The Lions, after all, have shown they can get after the quarterback. Led by edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson and interior lineman Alim McNeill, they are ranked third in the NFL with 27 sacks – 10.5 of those coming from the standout duo. The Patriots’ problems do not end with the talent Detroit has at its disposal. The team’s own personnel is also a question mark. On the one hand, you have an offensive line that will start yet another different combination along its interior with Ben Brown out at left guard. Greg Van Roten, who started one game in lieu of Mike Onwenu at right guard earlier in the year, and Walter Rouse, who only participated twice on a limited basis in practice this year, are the candidates to replace him, as are current right-side guard Matt Pryor and practice squad elevatee Andrew Rupcich. In addition, the status of running back Rhamondre Stevenson is also unclear. The sixth-year man suffered a knee injury last Sunday versus Green Bay and like Rouse only practiced twice as a limited participant this week. There are positive signs about his outlook – the Patriots did not elevate a running back to their game day roster – but how involved he will be especially in pass protection has yet to be seen. At the end of the day, the Patriots will need to find a way to get the job done regardless of the available personnel. Because if they do, their chances of moving the ball through the air do look good against a defense that has been vulnerable at times at the second and third levels.

title: Patriots’ first 5 international games, revisited before Lions matchup
summary: For the third time in the last four years, the New England Patriots have taken a trip abroad. On Sunday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will take on the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany. It will be the club’s second trip to Germany, and sixth international regular season game overall. In […]
full_text: For the third time in the last four years, the New England Patriots have taken a trip abroad. On Sunday, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel will take on the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany. It will be the club’s second trip to Germany, and sixth international regular season game overall. In total, the Patriots are entering that contest with a 3-2 record, even though they are coming off two straight defeats outside the United States With that said, let’s take a closer look at the Patriots’ international history. Patriots international games 2009 vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (London): The Patriots’ first non-preseason game on international soil took place at London’s Wembley Stadium during the 2009 season, and it was a blowout. Led by an opportunistic defense that had three interceptions — including a Brandon Meriweather pick-six — New England ended up beating Tampa Bay with a final score of 35-7. 2012 vs. St. Louis Rams (London): Three years after the Buccaneers were blown out by the Patriots at Wembley Stadium, the Rams suffered the same fate. While they did take a 7-0 lead, New England ended up scoring 45 unanswered after that. Tom Brady threw four touchdown passes en route to a 45-7 victory, with Rob Gronkowski as his favorite target: the two future Hall of Famers connected eight times for 146 yards and two scores. 2017 vs. Oakland Raiders (Mexico City): The Patriots’ first trip to Mexico in two decades — more on that in a second — saw them leave the Raiders no chance. Tom Brady threw three touchdowns this time around, while Stephen Gostkowski went 4-for-4 on field goal tries including a career-long from 62 yards out. When all was said and done, New England had scored 33 points to the Raiders’ 8, improving to 3-0 in international regular season games. 2023 vs. Indianapolis Colts (Frankfurt): The Patriots’ first game in Germany, an international marketing territory for them, was a debacle from start to finish. Cornerback J.C. Jackson was scratched from the trip, questions about Bill Belichick’s future started to get louder, and the contest itself was a low point even by the Patriots’ 2023 standards. Their 10-6 defeat was topped off by quarterbacks Mac Jones and Bailey Zappe both throwing head-scratching interceptions on back-to-back fourth-quarter drives to seal the defeat. 2024 vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (London): Their return to the United Kingdom for the first time in 12 years ended in a second straight international defeat for the Patriots. Drake Maye’s second career start saw him complete 70.3% of his passes for 276 yards and a pair of touchdowns, but his efforts were not enough to steady an uneven offense or overcome some shaky punt coverage and third down defense. When all was said and done, New England was beaten 32-16 to drop to 3-2 outside the United States. Patriots international exhibition games While those five games are the most notable, the Patriots’ international history is actually longer than that. In addition to those games, they also played three preseason contests plus an interleague game abroad over the course of the years. The first of those came in August 1969, when the then-Boston Patriots met the Lions at Jarry Park in Montreal in an AFL-NFL clash. The game ended 22-9 in the Lions’ favor. The Patriots also came up empty in their next trips to Canada. Facing the Pittsburgh Steelers at Montreal’s Olympic Stadium in the 1990 preseason, New England lost 30-14; three years after that, they were beaten 12-9 by the Cleveland Browns in Toronto. In 1998, they celebrated a 21-3 victory over the Dallas Cowboys in an exhibition showdown in Mexico City, as mentioned above. The team also was scheduled to take on the Seattle Seahawks in the so-called China Bowl in August 2007. That game, which would have taken place in Beijing, was initially postponed to 2009 before being canceled altogether.
